b: It refers to the original/root letters of the word, represented in morphological analysis by ف، ع، ل.

f: Why are فاء، عين، ولام used as the standard morphological measure?
b: The pattern ف-ع-ل is broader in meaning because all verbs contain the meaning of an action; it is also lighter than alternatives such as جَعَلَ.

f: Why is ف-ع-ل preferred over ج-ع-ل as the morphological measure?
b: فَعَلَ is lighter, and جَعَلَ itself has another meaning, such as “to create” or “to make,” whereas ف-ع-ل is therefore more suitable as a neutral morphological measure.

f: What additional feature makes ف-ع-ل suitable as the morphological measure?
b: Its letters represent the three principal articulation regions: the lips (الشفة), the middle of the mouth/throat region (الوسط), and the throat (الحلق).

f: Why is the basic triliteral verb (الثلاثي المجرد) considered the original category?
b: It is the original because it is free of additional letters and consists of exactly three original letters.

f: What are the possible vowel patterns of the basic triliteral past tense?
b: The past tense of a basic triliteral verb has the pattern فَعَلَ with fatḥah on the ʿayn, فَعِلَ with kasrah on the ʿayn, or فَعُلَ with ḍammah on the ʿayn.

f: Why is the fāʾ of the basic triliteral past tense always vowelled with fatḥah?
b: Because Arabic avoids beginning with a sākin, and fatḥah is considered the lightest of the three short vowels.

f: Why is the lām of the basic triliteral past tense vowelled with fatḥah?
b: The lām is vowelled with fatḥah according to the established pattern of the basic triliteral past tense, as will be explained in the text.

f: Why must the ʿayn of the basic triliteral past tense be vowelled?
b: Because leaving it sākin could result in the meeting of two sukūns (التقاء الساكنين), as in forms such as ضَرَبْتُ and ضَرَبْنَ.

f: Why are there only three possibilities for the vowel of the ʿayn?
b: Because the short vowels are limited to fatḥah, kasrah, and ḍammah.

f: What unusual forms such as نِعْمَ and شَهِدَ are mentioned in the discussion of triliteral verbs?
b: Forms such as نِعْمَ and شَهِدَ involve variations in the vowel of the fāʾ and/or ʿayn and are treated as departures from the basic pattern due to considerations of ease.

f: What is said to be the original pattern of نِعْمَ and similar forms with a ḥalqī ʿayn?
b: The text states that their original pattern is فَعِلَ with kasrah on the ʿayn.

f: How many linguistic variants are mentioned for this type of form?
b: Four variants are mentioned: kasrah on the fāʾ with sukūn on the ʿayn; kasrah on both; fatḥah on the fāʾ with sukūn on the ʿayn; and fatḥah on the fāʾ with kasrah on the ʿayn.

f: To what other words can these four variants apply?
b: They can occur with nouns or verbs on the pattern فَعِلَ whose ʿayn is one of the ḥurūf al-ḥalq (throat letters).

f: What are the two possible present-tense patterns of a basic triliteral verb whose past tense is فَعَلَ?
b: Its present tense may be يَفْعُلُ with ḍammah on the ʿayn, or يَفْعِلُ with kasrah on the ʿayn.

f: What is an example of فَعَلَ يَفْعُلُ?
b: نَصَرَ يَنْصُرُ.

f: What meanings can نَصَرَ have in the examples given?
b: نَصَرَهُ means “he helped him,” while نَصَرَ الغَيْثُ الأرضَ means “the rain aided/relieved the land,” i.e. brought it relief.

f: How does Abū ʿUbaydah explain the expression يَنْصُرْهُ in the cited Qur'anic verse?
b: He explains it as meaning يَرْزُقْهُ اللهُ—“that Allah will provide for him.”

f: What is an example of فَعَلَ يَفْعِلُ?
b: ضَرَبَ يَضْرِبُ.

f: What meanings of ضَرَبَ are mentioned in the examples?
b: ضَرَبَهُ بالسوط means “he struck him with a whip”; ضَرَبَ في الأرض means “he travelled/went through the land”; and ضَرَبَ مَثَلًا means “he presented/gave an example.”

f: When can a basic triliteral verb with فَعَلَ in the past have يَفْعَلُ with fatḥah in the present?
b: It can have يَفْعَلُ when either the ʿayn or lām of the verb is one of the six throat letters (حروف الحلق).

f: Why does the presence of a throat letter favor fatḥah on the ʿayn of the present tense?
b: The throat letters are among the heaviest letters, so the fatḥah on the ʿayn serves to counterbalance their heaviness.

f: What are the six throat letters (حروف الحلق)?
b: They are ء، ه، ع، ح، غ، خ: hamzah, hāʾ, ʿayn, ḥāʾ, ghayn, and khāʾ.

f: Why are the throat letters listed in the order الهمزة، الهاء، العين، الحاء، الغين، الخاء?
b: They are arranged according to their places of articulation, beginning with hamzah from the deepest part of the throat, followed by hāʾ, then the remaining letters according to their articulation points.

f: What is an example of a basic triliteral verb with a throat letter that has يَفْعَلُ in the present?
b: سَأَلَ يَسْأَلُ is an example.

f: What is another example of a basic triliteral verb with a throat letter that has يَفْعَلُ in the present?
b: مَنَعَ يَمْنَعُ is another example.

f: Does the presence of a throat letter in the ʿayn or lām always require fatḥah in the present tense?
b: No. The condition is sufficient to permit or account for the pattern, but its presence does not necessarily require the condition to occur. The existence of the condition does not entail the existence of the resulting pattern.

f: Which verbs demonstrate that a throat letter does not necessarily produce يَفْعَلُ?
b: Examples include دَخَلَ يَدْخُلُ, نَحَتَ يَنْحِتُ, and جَاءَ يَجِيءُ, despite having a throat letter in the relevant radical.

f: Why is أَبَى يَأْبَى considered anomalous (شاذّ)?
b: أَبَى يَأْبَى has fatḥah in the present despite not satisfying the stated condition for the pattern يَفْعَلُ, so it is treated as an exception to the regular قياس.

f: Does being described as شاذّ mean that a form is incorrect or unacceptable?
b: No. A form can be شاذّ with respect to the grammatical analogy while still occurring in eloquent Arabic and being accepted.

f: How many types of shudhūdh (الشذوذ) are mentioned?
b: Three types are mentioned: one that violates qiyās but not usage, one that violates usage but not qiyās, and one that violates both qiyās and usage.

f: Which types of shudhūdh are accepted?
b: The first two types are accepted: a form may conflict with analogy while being established in usage, or conflict with normal usage while conforming to analogy.

f: Which type of shudhūdh is rejected?
b: A form that conflicts with both established usage and grammatical analogy is rejected.

f: Why can the alif in أَبَى be not treated as a throat letter responsible for the fatḥah in يَأْبَى?
b: The text first rejects the premise that alif is one of the throat letters.

f: Why would attributing the fatḥah of أَبَى يَأْبَى to the alif create circular reasoning (الدور)?
b: Because the alif itself results from the original yāʾ being changed into alif due to its being vowelled and preceded by a fatḥah. If the fatḥah were itself caused by the alif, then the existence of the alif would depend on the fatḥah while the fatḥah depended on the alif, producing circularity.

f: Why did al-Zanjānī omit alif from the six throat letters?
b: Because in this context alif can only be an originally transformed wāw or yāʾ, and the purpose is to identify the consonant that causes fatḥah on the ʿayn—not a letter whose own existence depends upon that fatḥah.

f: What is the dialectal form قَلَى يَقْلَى mentioned in the passage?
b: قَلَى يَقْلَى with fatḥah in the present is reported as the language of Banū ʿĀmir; the more eloquent form has kasrah in the present.

f: What is the standard form of قَلَى in the present tense according to the passage?
b: The more eloquent form is قَلَى يَقْلِي with kasrah on the ʿayn of the present.

f: What is the dialectal form بَقِيَ يَبْقَى mentioned in the passage?
b: بَقِيَ يَبْقَى with fatḥah in the present is reported as the language of Ṭayyʾ.

f: What does the passage say about the original pattern of بَقِيَ?
b: Its original form has kasrah on the ʿayn of the past, but they changed it to fatḥah and changed the final lām into an alif for ease of pronunciation.

f: What is the explanation of رَكَنَ يَزْكَنُ?
b: It is regarded as a combination of two dialectal patterns: the past tense was taken from the pattern نَصَرَ يَنْصُرُ, while the present tense was taken from عَلِمَ يَعْلَمُ.

f: If a basic triliteral verb has the pattern فَعِلَ in the past, what is the normal pattern of its present tense?
b: Its present is normally يَفْعَلُ with fatḥah on the middle radical, e.g. عَلِمَ يَعْلَمُ.

f: What are examples of basic triliteral verbs that exceptionally have فَعِلَ يَفْعِلُ with kasrah in both the past and present?
b: Examples include حَسِبَ يَحْسِبُ and نَعِمَ يَنْعِمُ. This pattern is relatively rare in sound verbs but more common among weak verbs.

f: What are examples of weak verbs that exceptionally have kasrah in both the past and present?
b: Examples include وَرِثَ يَرِثُ، وَزِنَ يَزِنُ، وَوَرِعَ يَرِعُ، يَئِسَ يَيْئِسُ, and similar verbs.

f: Why does فَضِلَ يَفْضُلُ, نَعِمَ يَنْعُمُ, and مَاتَ يَمُوتُ involve a mixture of two morphological languages?
b: Their past tense follows the pattern of عَلِمَ يَعْلَمُ, while their present follows نَصَرَ يَنْصُرُ. Thus, the past was taken from one language and the present from another.

f: Why is مُتُّ pronounced with a kasrah on the mīm in ماتَ?
b: Its underlying form is مَوْتْتُ. The kasrah of the wāw is transferred to the preceding mīm, producing مِتُّ; the wāw is then deleted because two sukūns meet, with the second being the doubled tāʾ.

f: What is the standard pattern of the fifth basic triliteral verb category, فَعُلَ?
b: Its present normally follows يَفْعُلُ, with ḍammah on the middle radical, e.g. حَسُنَ يَحْسُنُ.

f: What kind of meanings are typically expressed by verbs on فَعُلَ يَفْعُلُ?
b: This category is generally used for inherent or permanent qualities and is therefore normally intransitive, e.g. الحُسن، الكَرَم، القُبح and similar qualities.

f: Why were ḍammah and ḍammah chosen for فَعُلَ يَفْعُلُ?
b: Because these qualities are associated with a pattern whose pronunciation involves the joining of the lips, creating a correspondence between the sound of the form and its meanings.

f: What exceptional usage is found in رَحُبَتْكَ الدارُ?
b: The standard construction is رَحُبَتْ بِكَ الدارُ (“the house became spacious for you”). The preposition بـ may be omitted because of frequent usage and abbreviation.

f: What is the pattern of the basic quadriliteral verb (الرباعي المجرد)?
b: It follows فَعْلَلَ, with fatḥah on the first and final radicals, sukūn on the second radical, and fatḥah on the third, e.g. دَحْرَجَ. Its verbal noun is دَحْرَجَة or دِحْراج.

f: Why does the basic quadriliteral pattern have fatḥah on its first and final radicals and sukūn on the second?
b: The past tense begins and ends with fatḥah. The first of the two middle radicals cannot be left sākin when followed by another sākin in forms such as دَحْرَجْتُ and دَحْرَجْنَا, so it is given fatḥah. The second middle radical is made sākin because Arabic does not permit four consecutive moving letters in one word.

f: What are examples of verbs treated as belonging to the basic quadriliteral pattern through ilhāq (إلحاق)?
b: Examples include جَوْرَبَ، جَلْبَبَ، بَيْطَرَ، هَرْوَلَ، شَرِيفَ، دَلِيلَ. One indication of such classification is that their verbal nouns correspond to those of the quadriliteral pattern.

f: Into how many divisions is the augmented triliteral verb (الثلاثي المزيد فيه) divided?
b: It is divided into three sections, according to whether one, two, or three letters have been added to the basic triliteral root.

f: Which letters are normally used as augmenting letters in Arabic morphology?
b: They are the letters contained in سَأَلْتُمُونِيها. An exception is ilhāq and taḍʿīf, in which any letter may be added.

f: Why is the augmented triliteral verb divided according to one, two, or three added letters?
b: Because otherwise the derivative would possess an advantage over its original in a way that conflicts with the principle that the derivative should not exceed the original in structural simplicity.

f: What are the three patterns of augmented triliteral verbs whose past has four letters?
b: They are أَفْعَلَ، فَعَّلَ، فَاعَلَ. Examples are أَكْرَمَ إِكْرَامًا، فَرَّحَ تَفْرِيحًا، قَاتَلَ مُقَاتَلَةً وَقِتَالًا.

f: What are the principal meanings of the pattern أَفْعَلَ?
b: It may indicate causation/transitivity (أكرمته), becoming or acquiring a quality (أغدَّ البعير), finding something characterized by a quality (أحمدته), removal (أعجمت الكتاب), intensification/addition of meaning (شغلته وأشغلته), and exposing something to an action (أباع الجارية).

f: How does أَفْعَلَ indicate causation or transitivity?
b: It can make an intransitive or less-transitive meaning causative, e.g. أكرمته means “I honored him.”

f: How can أَفْعَلَ indicate that something has acquired the quality from which the verb is derived?
b: For example, أَغَدَّ البعيرُ means that the camel became one possessing غُدَّة (a gland/swelling), and أَصْبَحْنَا means “we entered the morning,” literally becoming associated with morning.

f: How can أَفْعَلَ indicate finding something characterized by a quality?
b: أَحْمَدْتُهُ means “I found him praiseworthy” or “I found him deserving of praise.”

f: How can أَفْعَلَ indicate removal or stripping away?
b: أَعْجَمْتُ الكتابَ means “I removed its ambiguity,” i.e. I made it clear or supplied its vowel/diacritical clarification.

f: How can أَفْعَلَ indicate exposing something to an action?
b: أَبَاعَ الجاريةَ means “he offered the slave-girl for sale,” i.e. he exposed her to the process of being sold.

f: Can a verb transferred to the pattern أَفْعَلَ become intransitive?
b: Yes. Examples include أَكَبَّ and أَعْرَضَ. كَبَّهُ means “he threw him face-down,” while أَكَبَّ means “he turned/fell face-down”; عَرَضَهُ means “he displayed it,” while أَعْرَضَ means “he turned away.” Al-Zawzanī states that these are the only two examples known to him of this phenomenon.

f: What is the pattern فَعَّلَ, and what is disputed concerning its doubled radical?
b: It is formed by doubling the middle radical, e.g. فَرَّحَ. There is disagreement over whether the first or second occurrence of the doubled radical is the added letter. Al-Khalīl preferred considering the first one added because a sākin is more appropriately regarded as additional than a moving letter; others preferred the second because addition at the end is more natural. Both analyses are permitted according to Sībawayh.

f: What are the principal meanings of فَعَّلَ?
b: It may indicate intensification/multiplicity in the action (جَوَّلَ، طَوَّفَ), multiplicity in the agent (مَوَّتَ الإبلَ), multiplicity in the object (غَلَّقَ الأبوابَ), attributing the object to the root meaning (فَسَّقَهُ), causation (فَرَّحَهُ), removal (جَلَّدَ البعيرَ, “removed its skin”), and other meanings.

f: How does فَعَّلَ indicate multiplicity in the action?
b: Examples include جَوَّلَ (“he went around repeatedly”) and طَوَّفَ (“he moved/went around repeatedly”).

f: How does فَعَّلَ indicate multiplicity in the agent?
b: مَوَّتَ الإبلَ indicates repeatedly or extensively causing the camels to die.

f: How does فَعَّلَ indicate multiplicity in the object?
b: غَلَّقَ الأبوابَ indicates closing the doors repeatedly or many doors.

f: How does فَعَّلَ indicate removal?
b: جَلَّدَ البعيرَ means “he removed the camel's skin,” from جلد.

f: What is the pattern فَاعَلَ, and what is its basic semantic function?
b: It is formed by adding an alif after the first radical, e.g. قَاتَلَ مُقَاتَلَةً وَقِتَالًا. Its basic usage indicates an action involving two or more parties, where each performs the action in relation to the other, e.g. ضَارَبَ زيدٌ عمرًا.

f: How does فَاعَلَ indicate reciprocity or participation between two parties?
b: In ضَارَبَ زيدٌ عمرًا, Zayd struck ʿAmr and ʿAmr struck Zayd. Thus, the form attributes the action to participants who interact with one another.

f: What other meanings can فَاعَلَ convey besides reciprocal action?
b: It may have the meaning of فَعَّلَ for intensification (ضَاعَفَ/ضَعَّفَ), the meaning of أَفْعَلَ (عَافَاكَ اللهُ

f: Into how many types is the augmented triliteral verb with a five-letter past divided?
b: It has two types, giving a total of five patterns in this section. The two types are تَفَعَّلَ and تَفَاعَلَ.

f: What is the pattern تَفَعَّلَ, and what are its principal meanings?
b: It is formed by adding تاء and doubling the middle radical, e.g. تَكَسَّرَ. It may indicate passive responsiveness (muṭāwaʿah) to فَعَّلَ, taking on a quality through effort, taking the object as the basis of the action, turning away from an action, repetition, and seeking/acquiring the root meaning.

f: How does تَفَعَّلَ express muṭāwaʿah of فَعَّلَ?
b: It indicates that the effect of a transitive action has occurred in the object, e.g. كَسَّرْتُهُ فَتَكَسَّرَ — “I broke it, and it became broken.”

f: What is meant by muṭāwaʿah (المطاوعة) in the pattern تَفَعَّلَ?
b: It is the occurrence of the effect produced by a transitive verb in its object. Thus, when one says كَسَّرْتُهُ, the resulting state is التكسّر: the object becomes broken.

f: How does تَفَعَّلَ indicate taking on a quality through effort or pretence?
b: تَحَلَّمَ means “he made an effort to acquire the quality of forbearance (الحِلم)” or deliberately acted with forbearance.

f: How does تَفَعَّلَ indicate taking the object as the basis or instrument of the action?
b: تَوَسَّدْتُهُ means “I took it as a pillow,” i.e. I made the object (وسادة) the basis of the action.

f: How can تَفَعَّلَ indicate turning away from an action?
b: تَهَجَّدَ indicates turning away from or separating oneself from الهجود (sleeping/resting), i.e. staying awake for night worship.

f: How can تَفَعَّلَ indicate repeated occurrence of the root action?
b: تَجَرَّعَهُ means that he drank it one mouthful/portion after another, indicating repetition of the action.

f: How can تَفَعَّلَ indicate seeking a quality?
b: تَكَبَّرَ can indicate seeking or attempting to be كبيرًا, i.e. seeking greatness.

f: What is the pattern تَفَاعَلَ, and what are its principal meanings?
b: It is formed by adding تاء and alif, e.g. تَبَاعَدَ. It can indicate an action performed by two or more participants, muṭāwaʿah of فَاعَلَ, and deliberate adoption or pretence of a quality.

f: How does تَفَاعَلَ indicate an action performed by two or more participants?
b: Examples include تَضَارَبَا and تَضَارَبُوا, meaning that the participants struck one another.

f: How does transitivity change when a verb on فَاعَلَ involving two objects is converted to تَفَاعَلَ?
b: A verb that is transitive to two objects in فَاعَلَ may become transitive to only one in تَفَاعَلَ. For example, نَازَعْتُهُ الحديثَ has two objects/participants, while تَنَازَعْتُهُ has one object.

f: Why does تَفَاعَلَ indicate participation rather than merely the action of one party toward another?
b: فَاعَلَ was established to attribute the action to a doer in relation to another party, while تَفَاعَلَ was established to attribute the action to the participants jointly, without specifically intending the relation of one participant's action to the other.

f: How does تَفَاعَلَ express muṭāwaʿah of فَاعَلَ?
b: For example, بَاعَدْتُهُ فَتَبَاعَدَ — “I made him distant, and he became distant.”

f: How does تَفَاعَلَ indicate deliberate pretence or adoption of a quality?
b: تَجَاهَلَ means “he deliberately acted ignorant,” despite the fact that ignorance was absent from him.

f: What is the distinction between the meaning of “taking on a quality through effort” in تَفَعَّلَ and the corresponding meaning in تَفَاعَلَ?
b: In تَفَعَّلَ, as in تَحَلَّمَ, the person seeks for the quality itself to become present in him. In تَفَاعَلَ, as in تَجَاهَلَ, he pretends to possess or display the quality even though it is actually absent from him.

f: What are the remaining five-letter patterns of augmented triliteral verbs whose first letter is hamzah?
b: They are اِنْفَعَلَ، اِفْتَعَلَ، اِفْعَلَّ.

f: What is the pattern اِنْفَعَلَ, and what is its principal function?
b: It is formed by adding الهمزة والنون, e.g. اِنْقَطَعَ انْقِطَاعًا. Its principal function is muṭāwaʿah of a basic triliteral verb.

f: How does اِنْفَعَلَ express muṭāwaʿah?
b: It expresses the occurrence of an effect produced by a transitive verb, e.g. قَطَعْتُهُ فَانْقَطَعَ — “I cut it, and it became cut.”

f: Why is the pattern اِنْفَعَلَ normally intransitive?
b: Because it is used for muṭāwaʿah, and muṭāwaʿah denotes the effect occurring in the object itself rather than an action being directed to another object.

f: Can اِنْفَعَلَ sometimes express muṭāwaʿah of أَفْعَلَ?
b: Yes, though this is described as shādh (exceptional), e.g. أَسْفَقْتُ البابَ فَانْسَفَقَ (“I pushed the door back, and it was pushed back”) and أَزْعَجْتُهُ فَانْزَعَجَ (“I drove him away, and he was driven away/disturbed”).

f: Why can verbs on اِنْفَعَلَ not normally be formed from every verb?
b: Because the pattern was restricted to muṭāwaʿah, so its base verb must involve an action or exertion (علاج وتأثير) whose effect can visibly occur. Therefore forms such as اِنْكَرَمَ and اِنْعَدَمَ are not normally constructed in this way.

f: What is the pattern اِفْتَعَلَ, and what are its principal meanings?
b: It is formed by adding الهمزة والتاء, e.g. اِجْتَمَعَ اجْتِمَاعًا. It may indicate muṭāwaʿah, taking/adopting something, intensification, the meaning of فَعَلَ, or the meaning of تَفَاعَلَ.

f: How does اِفْتَعَلَ express muṭāwaʿah?
b: For example, جَمَعْتُهُ فَاجْتَمَعَ — “I gathered it/them, and it became gathered.”

f: How can اِفْتَعَلَ indicate taking or adopting something?
b: اِخْتَبَزَ can mean اتخذ الخبز, “he took/adopted bread” (i.e. made bread for himself).

f: How can اِفْتَعَلَ indicate increased intensity or exaggeration?
b: اِكْتَسَبَ may indicate exerting oneself or going to considerable effort in acquiring something, i.e. intensification in الكسب.

f: When can اِفْتَعَلَ have the meaning of simple فَعَلَ?
b: In some verbs it simply conveys the meaning of the basic form, e.g. جَذَبَ وَاجْتَذَبَ.

f: When can اِفْتَعَلَ have the meaning of تَفَاعَلَ?
b: For example, اِخْتَصَمُوا can have the same meaning as تَخَاصَمُوا, “they disputed/quarreled with one another.”

f: What is the pattern اِفْعَلَّ, and what is its principal function?
b: It is formed by adding the hamzah and one of the lām letters, e.g. اِحْمَرَّ احْمِرَارًا. It indicates intensification, and is normally intransitive.

f: To what semantic categories is اِفْعَلَّ principally restricted?
b: It is especially used for colors and defects, e.g. اِحْمَرَّ (“became intensely red”).

f: What are the patterns of augmented triliteral verbs whose past has six letters?
b: They are اِسْتَفْعَلَ، اِفْعَالَّ، اِفْعَوْعَلَ، اِفْعَوَّلَ، اِفْعَنْلَلَ، اِفْعَنْلَى. Some of these are treated as regular patterns and some as forms attached by ilhāq.

f: What is the pattern اِسْتَفْعَلَ, and what are its principal meanings?
b: It is formed by adding الهمزة والسين والتاء, e.g. اِسْتَخْرَجَ اسْتِخْرَاجًا. It may indicate seeking the basic action, finding something characterized by it, transformation, or sometimes the meaning of فَعَلَ.

f: How does اِسْتَفْعَلَ indicate seeking the basic action?
b: اِسْتَخْرَجْتُهُ means “I sought/asked for its coming out” or “I caused it to come out,” understood from طلب خروجه.

f: How does اِسْتَفْعَلَ indicate finding something characterized by a quality?
b: اِسْتَعْظَمْتُهُ means “I found it great/magnificent,” i.e. وجدته عظيمًا.

f: How does اِسْتَفْعَلَ indicate transformation?
b: اِسْتَحْجَرَ الطينُ means “the clay became stone-like/turned into stone.”

f: Can اِسْتَفْعَلَ have the meaning of simple فَعَلَ?
b: Yes. For example, قَرَّ وَاسْتَقَرَّ may be equivalent in meaning. It has also been explained as retaining a sense of seeking, as though اِسْتَقَرَّ means that something seeks stability for itself.

f: What is the pattern اِفْعَالَّ, and how does its meaning compare with اِفْعَلَّ?
b: It is formed by adding الهمزة والألف واللام, e.g. اِحْمَارَّ احْمِيرَارًا. Its ruling is like اِحْمَرَّ, but it expresses greater intensification.

f: What is the pattern اِفْعَوْعَلَ, and what does it indicate?
b: It is formed by adding الهمزة والواو وإحدى العينين, e.g. اِعْشَوْشَبَتِ الأرضُ اعْشِيشَابًا, meaning that the land became abundant in grass. It indicates intensification.

f: What is an example of the pattern اِفْعَوَّلَ, and what does it mean?
b: اِجْلَوَّذَ (with verbal noun اجلِواذ) means that someone proceeded swiftly in traveling or hurried along.

f: What is the pattern اِفْعَنْلَلَ, and what does اِقْعَنْسَسَ mean?
b: It is formed by adding الهمزة والنون وإحدى اللامين. اِقْعَنْسَسَ means “he retreated/turned back.”

f: What is the pattern اِفْعَنْلَى, and what does اِسْلَنْقَى mean?
b: It is formed by adding الهمزة والنون والألف. اِسْلَنْقَى means “he lay on his back” or “fell onto his back.”

f: Which two six-letter patterns are treated as forms attached by ilhāq rather than ordinary members of the preceding patterns?
b: اِفْعَنْلَلَ and اِفْعَنْلَى are described as attached forms; the author notes that there is therefore no reason to place them straightforwardly among the preceding regular patterns.

f: What does the author say about تَفَعَّلَ and تَفَاعَلَ when they are forms of ilhāq to تَدَحْرَجَ?
b: They too can occur as forms attached to تَدَحْرَجَ, although the author did not distinguish these attached forms from the regular patterns in his presentation.

f: How many patterns does the augmented quadriliteral verb (الرباعي المزيد فيه) have?
b: It has three patterns: تَفَعْلَلَ، اِفْعَنْلَلَ، اِفْعَلَّ.

f: What is the pattern تَفَعْلَلَ for an augmented quadriliteral verb?
b: It is formed by adding تاء to the basic quadriliteral pattern, e.g. تَدَحْرَجَ تَدَحْرُجًا. The lām is given ḍammah to distinguish the pattern from the basic quadriliteral form.

f: What are examples of verbs on تَفَعْلَلَ through attachment (ilhāq)?
b: Examples include تَجَلْبَبَ (“he put on a jilbāb”), تَجَوْرَبَ (“he put on a sock”), تَفَيْهَقَ (“he spoke excessively”), تَرَهْوَكَ (“he strutted”), and تَمَسْكَنَ (“he displayed humility/poverty”).

f: What is the pattern اِفْعَنْلَلَ in the augmented quadriliteral?
b: It is formed by adding الهمزة والنون to the quadriliteral base, e.g. اِحْرَنْجَمَ احْرِنْجَامًا, meaning “he became crowded together.”

f: How does اِحْرَنْجَمَ express muṭāwaʿah?
b: حَرْجَمْتُ الإبلَ فَاحْرَنْجَمَتْ means “I gathered the camels together, and they became gathered together.”

f: What is the difference between the patterns اِقْعَنْسَسَ and اِحْرَنْجَمَ as augmented quadriliteral forms?
b: In اِقْعَنْسَسَ, repetition of the final radical (لام) is required, whereas in اِحْرَنْجَمَ it is not.

f: What morphological changes are prohibited in forms created by ilhāq?
b: Idghām and iʿlāl are not permitted in an attached form, because the attached form must resemble the pattern to which it is attached in its wording/form.

f: What is the pattern اِفْعَلَّ in the augmented quadriliteral?
b: It is formed by adding hamzah and lām, with sukūn on the fāʾ, fatḥah on the ʿayn, the first lām lightly pronounced with fatḥah, and the final lām doubled, e.g. اِقْشَعَرَّ اقْشِعْرَارًا.

f: What does اِقْشَعَرَّ mean?
b: اِقْشَعَرَّ جِلْدُهُ means “his skin became covered with goosebumps” or “he experienced a shiver/gooseflesh.”

f: What is a transitive verb (الفعل المتعدي)?
b: It is a verb whose action passes from the subject to a direct object, such as ضَرَبْتُ زَيْدًا. The act of striking passes from the subject to Zayd.

f: Why is a transitive verb also called واقعًا?
b: It is called واقعًا because its action falls upon the direct object.

f: What is an intransitive verb (الفعل اللازم)?
b: It is a verb whose action remains with the subject and does not pass to a direct object, e.g. حَسُنَ زَيْدٌ.

f: Why is an intransitive verb also called لازمًا and غير واقع?
b: It is called لازمًا because its action remains attached to the subject rather than passing beyond it, and غير واقع because its action does not fall upon a direct object.

f: Can the same verb sometimes be used both transitively and with a preposition?
b: Yes. For example, شَكَرْتُهُ and شَكَرْتُ لَهُ, or نَصَحْتُهُ and نَصَحْتُ لَهُ.

f: How does the author classify a verb that is used both directly with an object and with a preposition?
b: When the two usages have the same meaning, the author considers the verb transitive, with the lām regarded as an additional, regularly occurring particle, because the meaning with the lām is the same as without it. Transitivity and intransitivity are ultimately determined according to meaning.

f: By what two means can an intransitive basic triliteral verb normally be made transitive?
b: By doubling the middle radical (تضعيف العين), thereby moving it to باب التفعيل, or by adding hamzah, thereby moving it to باب الإفعال.

f: How does تفعيل make an intransitive basic triliteral verb transitive?
b: It doubles the middle radical. For example, فَرِحَ زَيْدٌ is intransitive, while فَرَّحْتُ زَيْدًا is transitive: “I made Zayd happy.”

f: How does إفعال make an intransitive basic triliteral verb transitive?
b: It adds the hamzah of أفعل. For example, جَلَسَ is intransitive, while أَجْلَسْتُهُ is transitive: “I made him sit.”

f: Can a preposition make an intransitive verb transitive?
b: Yes. This applies to verbs in the basic and augmented triliteral and quadriliteral forms. For example, ذَهَبَ and اِنْطَلَقَ are normally intransitive, but ذَهَبْتُ بِزَيْدٍ and اِنْطَلَقْتُ بِهِ make the action extend to the noun through the preposition بـ.

f: Why can a preposition make an otherwise intransitive verb effectively transitive?
b: Because prepositions were established to carry the meanings of verbs toward nouns, thereby connecting the action to the noun.

f: Does every preposition alter the lexical meaning of the verb when it makes it govern a noun?
b: No. The author notes that among the prepositions, بـ can alter the meaning of the verb in some contexts, as in ذَهَبْتُ بِهِ, whereas this is not the case in the same way with مَرَرْتُ بِهِ.

f: How does al-Mubarrad understand the meaning of the bāʾ that changes the meaning of a verb?
b: According to al-Mubarrad, the bāʾ of causative/transitive usage (باء التعدية) entails accompaniment between the subject and the object, because he understands it as meaning مَعَ (“with”).

f: How does Sībawayh analyze the bāʾ in expressions such as ذَهَبْتُ بِهِ?
b: Sībawayh says that the bāʾ in such expressions functions like the hamzah of أفعل and doubling (التضعيف). Thus ذَهَبْتُ بِهِ has the meaning أَذْهَبْتُهُ (“I took/carried him away”), although accompaniment may or may not be intended.

f: What is the difference between the bāʾ of transitivity and transitivity through hamzah or doubling according to Sībawayh?
b: With the bāʾ, accompaniment between the subject and object may either be present or absent. With hamzah and doubling, the meaning necessarily undergoes the corresponding transitive change.

f: Can multiple prepositions make one verb govern several nouns?
b: Yes. There is no restriction preventing several different prepositions from being associated with a single verb, provided that they do not have the same meaning in the same construction.

f: Why is مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ بِعَمْرٍو not permitted?
b: Because both occurrences of بـ have the same meaning and would therefore improperly combine two identical prepositional relations.

f: Why is مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ بِالْبَرِّيَةِ permitted?
b: Because the two bāʾs have different meanings: the first means passing by Zayd, while the second has the meaning في البرية (“in the wilderness”).

f: Can every basic triliteral verb be made transitive by adding hamzah or doubling its middle radical?
b: No. Not every verb accepts these transitive formations. Moving a basic triliteral verb into one of the derivative patterns is dependent upon samaʿ (established usage).

f: What examples illustrate that not every verb can simply be made transitive through hamzah or doubling?
b: One cannot arbitrarily say أَنْصَرْتُ زَيْدًا عَمْرًا or ذَهَّبْتُ خَالِدًا merely to make the corresponding verbs transitive. Such derivative forms must be established through usage.

f: What is the more precise definition of the transitivity being contrasted with intransitivity?
b: The verb must undergo a change in meaning through the added element, because transitivity and intransitivity in this technical discussion are determined according to meaning. Thus ذَهَبْتُ بِهِ involves a change in meaning, unlike مَرَرْتُ بِهِ.

f: Can every verb with a prepositional phrase technically be said to be “transitive” to that phrase?
b: In a broad sense, yes: one may say that a verb governs a jār wa-majrūr, an adverb, or another complement. However, this is not the technical sense of transitivity being discussed here, where transitivity is contrasted with intransitivity.

f: Why does ذَهَبْتُ بِهِ count as a meaningful change in the verb while مَرَرْتُ بِهِ does not?
b: Without the preposition, the verb denotes an event attributed to its subject. With a preposition, the event becomes related to its governed noun. In ذَهَبْتُ بِهِ, the bāʾ additionally changes the meaning to “I took/carried him away,” whereas in مَرَرْتُ بِهِ the bāʾ does not produce this type of lexical-semantic change.

f: What is the subject of the chapter فصل في أمثلة تصريف هذه الأفعال?
b: It discusses the morphological forms produced by conjugating the previously mentioned verbs, including the past, present, imperative, and other forms resulting from their ṣarf.

f: Why does the author begin the discussion of verb forms with the past tense?
b: He gives precedence to the past because the past time precedes the present and future in temporal order, and because the past is considered the basis for the present tense, which is formed by adding elements to it. What is produced through addition is derivative, while that from which it is derived is considered original.

f: How does the author define the past tense (الفعل الماضي)?
b: It is الفعل الذي دل على معنى وجد في الزمان الماضي — “the verb that indicates a meaning which occurred in past time.”

f: Which part of the definition of the past tense constitutes the genus?
b: The phrase الفعل الذي دل على معنى وجد functions as the genus, because it encompasses verbs generally.

f: What excludes forms other than the past tense from the definition of the past tense?
b: The phrase في الزمان الماضي excludes verbs whose indicated meaning is not located in past time.

f: What distinction does the author make between the two senses of “past” in his definition?
b: In الزمان الماضي, “past” is understood in its linguistic/ordinary temporal sense. In the earlier use describing the technical form, it refers to the technical morphological category. This prevents the definition from becoming circular.

f: Why does لَمْ يَضْرِبْ appear to challenge the definition of the past tense?
b: Because لم causes the present-tense verb يَضْرِبْ to indicate past time. Thus, superficially, لم يضرب appears to satisfy the definition of a past-tense verb.

f: How does the author answer the objection that لَمْ يَضْرِبْ should therefore count as a past tense?
b: He says that its indication of past time is accidental, arising from لم. The classification is based on the verb's original grammatical designation, and يَضْرِبْ remains a present-tense form.

f: Why does the definition of the past tense apparently fail to include نِعْمَ، بِئْسَ، لَيْسَ، عَسَى?
b: These forms are indeclinable/frozen forms (جوامد) rather than the past-tense forms intended in this chapter. The discussion concerns the past tense as one of the morphological forms obtained through conjugating verbs.

f: What does the author mean when he says that the intended past tense is one of the أمثلة الحاصلة من تصريف هذه الأفعال?
b: He means that the discussion concerns the past-tense pattern produced when the verbs under examination are conjugated, rather than every Arabic word that may happen to resemble or function like a past tense.

f: How does the author respond if the definition is understood as referring to the past tense in an unrestricted sense?
b: He explains that forms such as the jāmid verbs and certain contractual expressions may appear not to indicate past time in their ordinary usage, but their lack of past-time indication is accidental and does not negate their original grammatical classification.

f: What are examples of Arabic contractual expressions that have the form of a past tense but may not refer to past time?
b: Examples include بِعْتُ and similar ṣīghat al-ʿuqūd (contractual formulas), which are uttered to effect a present legal transaction rather than merely to report a past event.

f: Into what two categories is the past tense divided according to voice?
b: The past tense (الفعل الماضي) is either active (مبني للفاعل) or passive (مبني للمفعول).

f: How is the active past tense (الماضي المبني للفاعل) identified morphologically?
b: Its first vowel is fatḥah, or, more precisely, its first pronounced/moving letter has fatḥah.

f: Why does the definition say “its first moving letter” rather than simply “its first letter”?
b: In forms such as اِجْتَمَعَ and اِسْتَفْعَلَ, the first letter is the initial hamzah, but it is dropped in connected speech (في الدرج). The first moving letter is therefore the tāʾ in اِجْتَمَعَ, and it has fatḥah.

f: Why does the author use “or” in the definition “what has its first letter open, or its first moving letter open”?
b: The أو is for division between two cases, not for expressing uncertainty. The definition therefore includes something possessing either of these two characteristics.

f: Why is the first moving letter of the past tense given fatḥah?
b: Arabic rejects beginning a word with a sākin. In forms such as اِفْتَعَلَ and اِسْتَفْعَلَ, fatḥah on the first pronounced letter also avoids problematic sukūns, and fatḥah is the lightest of the short vowels.

f: Why is the final letter of the past tense normally fatḥah?
b: The past tense is fundamentally built (مبني), since being built is the original condition of verbs. Its final fatḥah is also associated with its resemblance to nouns in occupying the syntactic position of a noun, while fatḥah is chosen because it is the lightest vowel.

f: When does the final fatḥah of the past tense change from its normal form?
b: It changes when the final radical is weak, as in غَزَا and رَمَى, when a moving nominative pronoun is attached, as in ضَرَبْتُ and ضَرَبْنَ, or when the wāw of the plural pronoun is attached, as in ضَرَبُوا.

f: Why does the author say that the past tense is “built” rather than inflected?
b: Because building (البناء) is considered the original state of verbs, unlike nouns, which are generally subject to grammatical inflection.

f: Why is fatḥah the normal ending of the past tense?
b: Fatḥah is the lightest of the short vowels, and the past tense is therefore given this lightest vowel in its basic form.

f: What are the active past-tense forms of نَصَرَ for the third-person masculine?
b: نَصَرَ = he (one male) helped; نَصَرَا = the two males helped; نَصَرُوا = the male plural helped.

f: What are the active past-tense forms of نَصَرَ for the third-person feminine?
b: نَصَرَتْ = she helped; نَصَرَتَا = the two females helped; نَصَرْنَ = the female plural helped.

f: What are the active past-tense forms of نَصَرَ for the second-person masculine?
b: نَصَرْتَ = you (one male) helped; نَصَرْتُمَا = you two males helped; نَصَرْتُمْ = you male plural helped.

f: What are the active past-tense forms of نَصَرَ for the second-person feminine?
b: نَصَرْتِ = you (one female) helped; نَصَرْتُمَا = you two females helped; نَصَرْتُنَّ = you female plural helped.

f: What are the active past-tense forms of نَصَرَ for the first person?
b: نَصَرْتُ = I helped; نَصَرْنَا = we helped.

f: What is the function of the tāʾ in نَصَرَتْ?
b: The tāʾ of feminine marking (تاء التأنيث) indicates that the subject is feminine.

f: Why is the feminine marker in the past tense a tāʾ?
b: The tāʾ was added to indicate femininity, as also occurs with nouns, e.g. نَاصِرَة.

f: Why is the feminine tāʾ in the past tense normally sākin, whereas the corresponding tāʾ in nouns is moving?
b: The moving tāʾ was associated with nouns, while the sākin tāʾ was assigned to verbs, creating a distinction between the two. This also reflects the fact that the verb is heavier than the noun.

f: Why is the feminine tāʾ in نَصَرَتَا given a vowel?
b: In the dual, its sukūn would meet the sukūn of the following element, so it is given a vowel to avoid the meeting of two sukūns.

f: What do the alif and wāw in forms such as نَصَرَا and نَصَرُوا indicate?
b: They are markers of the dual and plural subject, respectively.

f: Why is an additional tāʾ used for second-person pronouns in the past tense?
b: Different tāʾs were introduced for the masculine addressee, feminine addressee, and first person, and they were all given vowels to prevent confusion with the tāʾ of feminine marking.

f: Why is the tāʾ of the first-person singular نَصَرْتُ given ḍammah?
b: Ḍammah is considered the strongest of the short vowels, and because the first person is given precedence, it was assigned the ḍammah.

f: Why is the tāʾ of the masculine second-person singular نَصَرْتَ given fatḥah?
b: It could not be given ḍammah because that would make it identical with the first person (نَصَرْتُ). Fatḥah is lighter and was therefore assigned to the masculine addressee.

f: Why is the tāʾ of the feminine second-person singular نَصَرْتِ given kasrah?
b: Kasrah remained for the feminine addressee after ḍammah was assigned to the first person and fatḥah to the masculine second person. Kasrah also corresponds to the feminine yāʾ in forms such as اِضْرِبِي, since kasrah is the vowel associated with yāʾ.

f: Why was the same form نَصَرْتُمَا used for both masculine and feminine dual addressees?
b: No separate form was established for the two genders in the dual. Instead, an additional mīm distinguishes the dual addressees from the corresponding third-person dual forms and differentiates the masculine and feminine contexts through the broader pronoun system.

f: Why is the vowel before the mīm in نَصَرْتُمَا and نَصَرْتُمْ a ḍammah?
b: The mīm is a labial letter like the wāw, so ḍammah, which is associated with the lips, is considered appropriate before it.

f: What pronoun is used for “we” in the past tense, and what is its relationship to the independent pronoun?
b: The first-person plural uses نَا, as in فَعَلْنَا, corresponding to the independent pronoun نَحْنُ.

f: How are the third-person masculine and feminine plurals distinguished in the past tense?
b: The masculine plural is marked by wāw, as in نَصَرُوا, while the feminine plural is marked by nūn, as in نَصَرْنَ.

f: Why was the wāw assigned to the masculine plural and the nūn to the feminine plural?
b: The wāw is heavier/stronger than the nūn because it is one of the letters of madd and līn. It was therefore regarded as more suitable for the masculine, which is given precedence over the feminine.

f: How does the distinction between masculine and feminine plural appear in the second person?
b: The masculine plural is marked by mīm, as in نَصَرْتُمْ, while the feminine plural is marked by nūn, as in نَصَرْتُنَّ.

f: Why is mīm assigned to the masculine second-person plural?
b: It corresponds appropriately to the wāw, which marks the masculine third-person plural in the past tense (نَصَرُوا).

f: Why is nūn assigned to the feminine second-person plural?
b: It corresponds to the nūn used for the feminine third-person plural, as in نَصَرْنَ.

f: Why is the nūn in نَصَرْتُنَّ doubled?
b: The author explains that its original form was نَصَرْتُمْنَ. The mīm assimilated into the following nūn through obligatory idghām, producing the doubled nūn of نَصَرْتُنَّ.

f: Why is the tāʾ before the doubled nūn in نَصَرْتُنَّ given ḍammah?
b: The tāʾ is given ḍammah because of its association with the preceding mīm: the original sequence was تُمْنَ, and the ḍammah of the mīm is retained in the tāʾ before the mīm's assimilation into the nūn.

f: Are all these pronoun forms determined by phonetic reasoning alone?
b: No. The author concludes that although scholars mention various phonetic and semantic correspondences, ultimately these grammatical forms are established by the original واضع (language-establisher).

f: Is the wāw of the third-person masculine plural ever omitted?
b: Yes, though this is rare. The author cites the poetic example فَلَوْ أَنَّ الأَطِبَّاءَ كَانَ حَوْلِي وَكَانَ مَعَ الأَطِبَّاءِ الشُّفَاةُ, where كَانَ occurs in place of the expected كَانُوا, with the plural wāw omitted.

f: How are the past-tense conjugation patterns applied to the Arabic verb forms أفعل، فعّل، فاعل، فعلل، تفعلل، افتعل، انفعل، استفعل، افعلل، وافعوعل?
b: Each of these verb patterns is conjugated according to the same person-and-number sequence demonstrated for نصر. Thus, once the complete conjugation of one pattern is understood, the corresponding forms of the other patterns follow by analogy.

f: How is the past tense of the verb اقشعرّ conjugated in the third-person masculine?
b: اقشعرّ، اقشعرّا، اقشعرّوا: third-person masculine singular, dual, and plural respectively.

f: How is the past tense of the verb اقشعرّ conjugated in the third-person feminine?
b: اقشعرّت، اقشعرّتا، اقشعررن: third-person feminine singular, dual, and plural respectively.

f: How is the past tense of the verb اقشعرّ conjugated in the second-person masculine?
b: اقشعررتَ، اقشعررتما، اقشعررتم: second-person masculine singular, dual, and plural respectively.

f: How is the past tense of the verb اقشعرّ conjugated in the second-person feminine?
b: اقشعررتِ، اقشعررتما، اقشعررتن: second-person feminine singular, dual, and plural respectively.

f: How is the past tense of the verb اقشعرّ conjugated in the first person?
b: اقشعررتُ، اقشعررنا: first-person singular and plural respectively.

f: How is the past tense of the verb اعشوشب conjugated in the third-person masculine and feminine forms?
b: The masculine forms are اعشوشب، اعشوشبا، اعشوشبوا; the feminine forms are اعشوشبت، اعشوشبتا، اعشوشبن. The remaining persons follow the same conjugational pattern.

f: Why does the author give a complete conjugation of اقشعرّ but not complete conjugations of every other verb pattern?
b: Because the other verb patterns follow the same conjugational procedure. Giving one complete example is sufficient for an intelligent student to understand the remaining patterns, so multiplying examples unnecessarily does not improve understanding.

f: Which initial letters are excluded when determining the vowel of the beginning of forms such as افتعل، انفعل، واستفعل?
b: The initial hamzahs of hamzat al-waṣl are not considered when determining the vowel of the beginning, because they are extra letters used only to permit pronunciation of a word that would otherwise begin with a consonant carrying sukūn.

f: Why are the initial hamzahs in افتعل، انفعل، واستفعل considered extra letters?
b: They are added because Arabic does not permit beginning speech with a consonant carrying sukūn. They therefore serve as a phonetic means of beginning pronunciation rather than as part of the underlying morphological pattern.

f: Why are the initial hamzahs of افتعل، انفعل، واستفعل pronounced when these words begin speech?
b: They are pronounced at the beginning of speech because the speaker needs them in order to avoid beginning with a consonant carrying sukūn.

f: Why are the initial hamzahs of افتعل، انفعل، واستفعل omitted when these words occur in connected speech?
b: They are hamzat al-waṣl, so once the preceding word supplies a preceding vowel sound, there is no need for the hamzah. It therefore drops in connected speech.

f: Why is the initial hamzah of أفعل different from the initial hamzahs of افتعل، انفعل، واستفعل?
b: The hamzah of أفعل is hamzat al-qaṭʿ, so it does not drop in connected speech. The hamzahs of افتعل، انفعل، واستفعل are hamzāt al-waṣl and therefore do drop in connected speech.

f: Why does the author refer to the initial hamzahs as “alifs”?
b: Because an initial hamzah is written in the form of an alif. The author therefore uses “alif” in reference to its written form, even though technically the letter is a hamzah.

f: What distinction does the author quote from al-Ṣiḥāḥ concerning the alif and hamzah?
b: Al-Ṣiḥāḥ distinguishes between the weak alif, which is called ألف, and the moving alif-form, which is called همزة.

f: What is the general definition of المبني للمفعول?
b: المبني للمفعول is the verb الذي لم يسم فاعله, meaning a verb whose doer is not named.

f: Does the definition الفعل الذي لم يسم فاعله apply only to the passive past tense?
b: No. It is a general definition of the passive construction and applies to both the past and present passive.

f: Why can the doer be omitted from an Arabic passive construction?
b: The doer may be omitted to honor him, to disparage him, because he is unknown, because the identity of the doer is irrelevant, because the speaker intends the action to be attributed to any doer whatsoever, or for other rhetorical purposes discussed in ʿilm al-maʿānī.

f: Why is زيد grammatically raised in ضُرب زيد?
b: Because the original doer has been omitted, so زيد takes its place as نائب الفاعل and is therefore raised.

f: Why can the doer be omitted in a sentence such as قُتل الخارجي?
b: The important information may be that the khārijite was killed rather than who killed him; therefore there is no communicative need to mention the doer.

f: What objection can be made to defining the passive as الفعل الذي لم يسم فاعله?
b: The definition could also apply to an active verb when its subject is omitted in a construction where such omission is permitted. Therefore, the definition is not sufficient by itself to identify the specific morphological passive form.

f: What is the morphological definition of the passive past tense in Arabic according to the author?
b: The passive past tense is a past verb whose first letter is ḍammah, such as ضُرب، دُحرج، أُفعل، فُعّل، فُوعل، وتُفُعّل.

f: What is the passive past pattern corresponding to the active basic triliteral pattern فَعَلَ?
b: Its passive pattern is فُعِلَ, with ḍammah on the first radical and kasrah on the radical before the final radical.

f: What is the passive past pattern corresponding to the quadriliteral verb دَحْرَجَ?
b: Its passive pattern is دُحْرِجَ, with ḍammah on the first radical and kasrah before the final radical.

f: What is the passive past pattern corresponding to أَفْعَلَ?
b: Its passive pattern begins with ḍammah and has kasrah before the final radical, e.g. أُكرِمَ.

f: What is the passive past pattern corresponding to فَعَّلَ?
b: Its passive pattern is فُعِّلَ, with ḍammah on the first radical and kasrah before the final radical.

f: What is the passive past pattern corresponding to فَاعَلَ?
b: Its passive pattern is فُوعِلَ, with the initial vowel changed to ḍammah and the radical before the final radical carrying kasrah.

f: What is the passive past pattern corresponding to تَفَعَّلَ?
b: Its passive pattern is تُفُعِّلَ, with ḍammah on the tāʾ and the first radical, followed by kasrah before the final radical.

f: Why is the first moving letter of تَفَعَّلَ changed to ḍammah in its passive form?
b: The passive requires a change that distinguishes it from the active form. Therefore تَفَعَّلَ becomes تُفُعِّلَ.

f: Why is the passive form of تفاعل pronounced تُفُوعِلَ rather than merely changing the tāʾ to ḍammah?
b: The fāʾ is also given ḍammah, and the original alif is changed into wāw because it follows a ḍammah, producing تُفُوعِلَ. If only the tāʾ were changed, the form could be confused with the corresponding present active pattern.

f: Why is the initial moving letter of passive forms such as اُفتُعِلَ and اُستُفعِلَ given ḍammah?
b: In forms beginning with hamzat al-waṣl, the first moving letter after the initial hamzah is given ḍammah in the passive. Thus افتعل becomes اُفتُعِلَ, and استفعل becomes اُستُفعِلَ.

f: Why is the hamzat al-waṣl in a passive form such as اُستُخرِجَ pronounced with ḍammah?
b: Hamzat al-waṣl follows the ḍammah of the first moving letter, so when the word begins speech it is pronounced اُستُخرِجَ.

f: What vowel does the letter immediately before the final radical normally receive in the passive past tense?
b: It normally receives kasrah, as in ضُرِبَ، دُحرِجَ، أُكرِمَ، استُخرِجَ.

f: Why does the passive past tense use ḍammah on the first moving letter and kasrah before the final radical?
b: The change is necessary to distinguish the passive from the active. The basic active pattern فَعَلَ is changed to فُعِلَ by ḍammah on the first radical and kasrah on the second. Other patterns are then made to follow this arrangement consistently.

f: Why is the sequence of ḍammah followed by kasrah preferred in the passive rather than kasrah followed by ḍammah?
b: Both arrangements could theoretically distinguish the passive from the active, but moving from ḍammah to kasrah is preferable because it moves from a heavier vowel to a lighter one, thereby seeking ease after heaviness.

f: Why is the passive pattern فُعِلَ specifically preferred over other possible vowel patterns?
b: It distinguishes the passive from the active while also distancing the form from common noun patterns. The remaining non-triliteral forms are then made to follow the same pattern for consistency throughout the morphological system.

f: Why is the claim that the passive ḍammah compensates for the omitted subject rejected?
b: Because the raised نائب الفاعل already compensates for the omitted subject. There is therefore no need to regard the ḍammah itself as compensation for the omitted doer.

f: What are some non-standard dialectal or transmitted passive forms mentioned by the author?
b: Examples include فَزِدَ له with sukūn on the zāy, ضُرِبَ with the kasrah transferred to the first radical in one dialectal report, عُصْرَ with sukūn before the final radical, and the Qurʾānic reading رُدَّت with kasrah on the rāʾ.

f: How does the form فَزِدَ له arise according to the author's explanation?
b: Its underlying form is فَصَدَ له. The ṣād was first made sākin and then changed into zāy, yielding فَزْدَ له.

f: What example does Quṭrub report of transferring the kasrah in a passive verb?
b: He reports ضِرِبَ with the kasrah of the second radical transferred to the first radical, rather than the standard ضُرِبَ.

f: What unusual passive form involving عصر is mentioned by the author?
b: A form عُصْرَ is reported with sukūn on the radical before the final radical.

f: What non-standard Qurʾānic reading of رُدَّت is mentioned?
b: A reading رِدَّت is reported with kasrah on the rāʾ. The author regards such forms as exceptional and does not consider them sufficient to invalidate the general morphological rule.

f: Why does the author not regard exceptional forms such as رِدَّت as refutations of the standard passive rule?
b: Because they are rare transmitted usages or dialectal variants and therefore do not overturn the established morphological pattern.

f: Which verbs are mentioned as being permanently used in the passive because their doer is ordinarily understood?
b: The author mentions جُنَّ، عُلَّ، سُلَّ، قُدَّ، زُكِمَ، حُمَّ، وُعِكَ، شُلَّ، فُئِدَ، جُبِلَ and similar expressions.

f: Why can verbs such as جُنَّ، عُلَّ، سُلَّ، زُكِمَ، حُمَّ and وُعِكَ be used in the passive without naming a doer?
b: Because in ordinary usage the doer is generally understood to be Allah, so there is normally no need to state the doer explicitly.

f: Why does the author discuss the present tense (الفعل المضارع) immediately after discussing the past tense (الفعل الماضي)?
b: Because the imperative (الأمر) is a branch of the present tense, and the active and passive participles (اسم الفاعل واسم المفعول) are derived from the present/past verbal system.

f: What is the author's basic morphological definition of the Arabic present tense (الفعل المضارع)?
b: It is a verb that begins with one of the four additional letters: الهمزة، والنون، والتاء، والياء.

f: What mnemonic expressions are used to remember the four present-tense prefixes الهمزة، والنون، والتاء، والياء?
b: They are gathered in expressions such as أنيت، أتين، نأتي.

f: What does the initial hamzah (همزة) indicate in the Arabic present tense?
b: It indicates the first-person singular, i.e. the speaker alone, as in أنا أنصر.

f: What does the initial nūn (نون) indicate in the Arabic present tense?
b: It indicates the first person when accompanied by others, as in نحن ننصر. It can also be used for the singular speaker in contexts of emphasis or grandeur, as in نحن نقص عليك.

f: What does the initial tāʾ (تاء) indicate in the Arabic present tense?
b: It is used for the second person—masculine or feminine, singular, dual, or plural—and for the third-person feminine singular and dual, as in أنت تنصر، أنتما تنصران، أنتم تنصرون، أنتِ تنصرين، هي تنصر، وهما تنصران.

f: What does the initial yāʾ (ياء) indicate in the Arabic present tense?
b: It is used for the third-person masculine singular, dual, and plural, and for the third-person feminine plural, as in هو ينصر، هما ينصران، هم ينصرون، هن ينصرن.

f: Why is the definition “a verb beginning with one of the four letters أ، ن، ت، ي” not by itself sufficient to define the present tense?
b: Because past verbs such as أكرم، تكسر، تباعد also begin with one of these letters. The intended letters are specifically the prefixes used to mark the persons of the present tense.

f: Which hamzah is intended when the author says that the initial hamzah is a sign of the present tense?
b: The hamzah that indicates the first-person singular, as in أنا أنصر. It is not every hamzah that happens to occur at the beginning of a verb.

f: Which nūn is intended when the author says that the initial nūn is a sign of the present tense?
b: The nūn that indicates the first person together with another person, as in نحن ننصر.

f: Which tāʾ is intended when the author says that the initial tāʾ is a sign of the present tense?
b: The tāʾ that marks the second person or the third-person feminine singular or dual, such as أنت تنصر، أنتِ تنصرين، هي تنصر، هما تنصران.

f: Which yāʾ is intended when the author says that the initial yāʾ is a sign of the present tense?
b: The yāʾ that marks the third person, specifically the masculine singular, dual, and plural and the feminine plural, such as هو ينصر، هما ينصران، هم ينصرون، هن ينصرن.

f: Why were the four letters أ، ن، ت، ي chosen as prefixes for the Arabic present tense?
b: Because adding letters produces heaviness, so Arabic needed suitable letters for distinguishing the present from the past. The letters of madd and līn were considered especially suitable because they occur frequently in Arabic, either as themselves or through their corresponding three short vowels.

f: Why was the letter alif changed into hamzah for the first-person present-tense prefix?
b: Arabic rejects beginning a word with a consonant carrying sukūn, so the alif was changed into hamzah, whose articulation is close to that of alif.

f: Why was the hamzah assigned to the first-person singular in the present tense?
b: The speaker is considered first in the order of speech, and the articulation point of hamzah is also the first among the relevant articulation points, since it comes from the deepest part of the throat.

f: Why was wāw changed into tāʾ for the second-person present-tense prefix?
b: Adding wāw would produce excessive phonetic heaviness, especially in combinations such as وَوَجِلَ. Wāw is also frequently changed into tāʾ in Arabic, as in تراث and تجاه, whose underlying forms are وراث and وجاه.

f: Why was the tāʾ assigned to the second person in the present tense?
b: The second person comes after the speaker in the order of speech, so the tāʾ was assigned to it after the hamzah had been assigned to the speaker.

f: Why is the yāʾ associated with the third person in the present tense?
b: The articulation point of yāʾ is at the lips, and it represents the remaining third-person category after the prefixes for the speaker and addressee have been assigned.

f: Why is the present-tense prefix tāʾ used for the third-person feminine singular and dual?
b: It was assigned to these forms so that the feminine third-person forms would not become confused with the masculine third-person forms if they also used yāʾ. The distinction is then preserved through endings such as ون and ن in the plural.

f: Why does the third-person feminine plural use yāʾ rather than tāʾ as its present-tense prefix?
b: The yāʾ is more appropriate to the third-person category. Its articulation point is also intermediate between the articulation points associated with hamzah and wāw, and the third person occupies the position between speaker and addressee in the organization of speech.

f: Why does the third-person masculine plural use ياء in يضربون, while the third-person feminine plural uses ياء in يضربن but differs in its ending?
b: Both are third-person forms and therefore take the yāʾ prefix, but their plural endings distinguish masculine and feminine: يضربون for masculine plural and يضربن for feminine plural.

f: Why was nūn added as a present-tense prefix when the past tense already distinguished the speaker from others?
b: The past tense distinguished the speaker alone from the speaker together with others, so the present tense needed a corresponding distinction. Nūn was chosen because it resembles the letters of madd and līn in qualities such as subtlety and nasalization.

f: Why is the present tense called مضارع?
b: مضارع linguistically means “resembling” or “similar.” The present tense resembles other forms in several respects, as though the two similar things had nursed from one breast.

f: In what way does the Arabic present tense resemble اسم الفاعل?
b: It resembles اسم الفاعل in its pattern of vowels and sukūns.

f: In what way does the Arabic present tense resemble an indefinite noun?
b: Like an indefinite noun, the present tense can initially be shared by multiple possible referents; additional elements can then restrict its meaning.

f: How does the Arabic present tense resemble a noun through the use of السين، وسوف، واللام?
b: The present tense can be specified by particles such as السين، وسوف، واللام, just as an indefinite noun such as رجل may refer to any man until the definite article restricts it to الرجل.

f: Why is the Arabic present tense grammatically declinable (معرب) while the other basic verb forms are generally indeclinable?
b: Because the present tense has a particularly complete resemblance to the noun. This similarity is considered sufficient to make it muʿrab, unlike the other verb forms.

f: What two times can the Arabic present tense express?
b: It can express the present (الحال) and the future (الاستقبال).

f: What does الحال mean when the present tense is used for the present time?
b: It refers to portions of time around the boundary between past and future whose successive moments follow one another without a significant interval. What counts as the present is determined by customary usage.

f: What does الاستقبال mean when the present tense is used for the future?
b: It refers to something whose occurrence is expected after the time in which the speaker currently exists.

f: What is the difference between يفعل الآن and يفعل غدًا in terms of tense?
b: يفعل الآن expresses the present and is called حالًا or حاضرًا, while يفعل غدًا expresses the future and is called مستقبلًا.

f: Is المستقبل grammatically an active or passive participle?
b: The author states that the commonly used pronunciation المستقبَل with fatḥah on the bāʾ treats it as a passive participle, but the more correct form is المستقبِل, with kasrah on the bāʾ, because the subject itself “receives” or awaits the future.

f: Why might المستقبَل with fatḥah on the bāʾ be understood as a passive participle?
b: Because the time is something that we receive/encounter in the future, so it can be understood as the object that is received. However, the author considers المستقبِل with kasrah to be preferable.

f: What are the three positions concerning whether the Arabic present tense fundamentally indicates the present or the future?
b: One view says the present tense is fundamentally for the present, and its future use is figurative. Another says it is fundamentally for the future, and its present use is figurative. The preferred view is that it is shared between both meanings.

f: What evidence suggests that the present meaning is more fundamental when the present tense is used without a contextual indicator?
b: When the present tense is used without any contextual indication, understanding ordinarily moves first toward the present meaning, which suggests that the present is its original or more immediate meaning.

f: What particles can specifically mark the future with the Arabic present tense?
b: The particles سـ and سوف specifically indicate future time when attached to the present tense, as in سيفعل and سوف يفعل.

f: Why are سـ and سوف called the particles of تنفيس?
b: تنفيس means widening or giving more temporal room. These particles move the action away from the immediate present into the future, thereby “expanding” the temporal scope.

f: What is the difference between سـ and سوف in expressing the future?
b: Both indicate future time, but سوف provides a greater degree of تنفيس, meaning a greater temporal distance or extension than the shorter سـ.

f: What shortened forms of سوف are mentioned by the author?
b: The author mentions سو by deletion of the fāʾ, سي by changing the wāw into yāʾ, and سفعل by deleting the wāw and leaving the originally moving fāʾ in a position requiring the resulting phonetic adjustment.

f: Why might سـ be regarded as a shortened form of سوف?
b: Some scholars regard سـ as a reduced form of سوف, with the reduction of letters symbolically indicating that the action is temporally closer.

f: What does the use of سـ or سوف do to a present-tense verb such as يفعل?
b: It restricts the verb to the future, producing سيفعل or سوف يفعل, rather than leaving it capable of expressing either the present or future.

f: What is the effect of لام الابتداء on a present-tense verb such as يفعل according to the view mentioned by the author?
b: According to the cited view, when لام الابتداء enters upon a present tense that could mean either present or future, it makes the verb specifically indicate the present, as in ليفعل.

f: How does the Qurʾānic expression إني ليحزنني illustrate the use of لام الابتداء with the present tense?
b: The lām in ليحزنني emphasizes the present-tense verb and, according to the view discussed, gives it a present-time interpretation.

f: Why does لام الابتداء not necessarily indicate the present in expressions such as ولسوف يعطيك ربك فترضى?
b: Because the verb has already been restricted to the future by سوف. The lām therefore functions for emphasis rather than adding a present-time meaning.

f: How is the lām understood in ولسوف يعطيك ربك فترضى?
b: It is understood as a lām of emphasis, while سوف supplies the future meaning. The lām no longer contributes a present-time restriction.

f: How is the lām understood in ولسوف أخرج حيا?
b: As a lām of emphasis, because سوف has already made the verb purely future.

f: How is the lām understood in the Qurʾānic expression وإن ربك ليحكم بينهم يوم القيامة according to the author's discussion?
b: It is treated as an emphatic lām, while the future event is presented in the position of something like the present because its occurrence is certain.

f: What is the Basran grammatical position concerning the lām in expressions such as ليحكم?
b: According to the Basrans, the lām is fundamentally for emphasis, rather than being intrinsically a particle that makes the present tense indicate the present.

f: Why can the present tense be used for both present and future without being considered two separate verb forms?
b: Because the same present-tense form is shared between the two temporal meanings. Context determines whether the intended action is occurring now or is expected later, while particles such as سـ and سوف can explicitly restrict it to the future.

f: What are the two basic categories of the Arabic present tense (الفعل المضارع) according to whether the doer is named?
b: The present tense is either مبني للفاعل (active) or مبني للمفعول (passive).

f: What is the general rule for the initial present-tense prefix (حرف المضارعة) in an active present verb?
b: In an active present verb, the present-tense prefix is generally fatḥah, except when the corresponding past tense has four letters, in which case the present-tense prefix is ḍammah.

f: Which present-tense prefixes are generally opened with fatḥah in an active present verb?
b: The present-tense prefixes أ، ن، ت، ي are generally given fatḥah in active present verbs, as in ينصر، تنصر، أنصر، ننصر.

f: When is the present-tense prefix given ḍammah in an active present verb?
b: It is given ḍammah when the corresponding past tense has four letters, as in يدحرج، يكرم، يقاتل، يفرح.

f: What happens to the present-tense prefix of the active present forms of دحرج، أكرم، قاتل، وفرح?
b: It is given ḍammah: يدحرج، يكرم، يقاتل، يفرح.

f: Why is fatḥah the basic vowel of the present-tense prefix in an active present verb?
b: Because fatḥah is lighter than ḍammah, and the basic principle is to prefer the lighter vowel.

f: Why is the present-tense prefix of a verb such as يكرم given ḍammah rather than fatḥah?
b: If it were opened, يكرم could become indistinguishable from the present of a basic triliteral verb, creating ambiguity as to whether the verb is basic or augmented.

f: Why is ḍammah used for the present-tense prefix of all four-letter past verbs rather than only for أكرم?
b: The rule is generalized to all verbs whose past tense has four letters, such as يدحرج، يكرم، يقاتل، يفرح, so that the morphological category remains consistent.

f: Why is it preferable to assign ḍammah to the present-tense prefixes of four-letter past verbs rather than to assign fatḥah to them and tolerate ambiguity in one case?
b: Assigning ḍammah to all four-letter past verbs avoids ambiguity completely, whereas assigning fatḥah would create ambiguity in at least one form, such as يكرم.

f: Why is ḍammah assigned to the smaller category of four-letter past verbs while fatḥah is assigned to the larger category?
b: Because ḍammah is heavier than fatḥah, so the heavier vowel is assigned to the smaller group and the lighter vowel to the larger group, producing a balance between the two.

f: How does the rule for the active present-tense prefix account for أهراق يُهريق?
b: أهراق يُهريق does not conform literally to the general rule because its present-tense prefix is ḍammah even though its apparent past form is not four letters. It can be explained by treating the additional hāʾ as an irregular extra letter, so that the verb is effectively treated as four-lettered for this rule, or by classifying it as an exceptional form.

f: How does the rule for the active present-tense prefix account for أسطاع يُسطيع?
b: أسطاع يُسطيع similarly has an apparent exception because its present-tense prefix is ḍammah. Its additional sīn may be treated as an irregular addition, making the form effectively four-lettered for purposes of the rule, or it may simply be classified among the exceptional forms.

f: What are the underlying basic verbs associated with أهراق and أسطاع?
b: أهراق is associated with أراق, while أسطاع is associated with أطاع; the hāʾ and sīn are additional letters outside the normal pattern.

f: Why can exceptional forms such as يُهريق and يُسطيع be excluded from a morphological definition?
b: Because a technical definition need not necessarily encompass irregular or anomalous forms (الشواذ) that fall outside the regular morphological system.

f: Why does the present-tense prefix remain opened in يَخْصِم and يَقْتُل when these forms are derived from verbs whose apparent past forms have more than three letters?
b: Forms such as يَخْصِم and يَقْتُل originate from اختصم and اقتتل. Through deletion of the initial hamzah and assimilation of the tāʾ into the following consonant, they are treated as having five letters underlyingly, so their present-tense prefixes remain fatḥah.

f: What are the underlying forms of the present verbs يَخْصِم and يَقْتُل mentioned by the author?
b: يَخْصِم derives from اختصم, and يَقْتُل derives from اقتتل. The tāʾ of the افتعال pattern is assimilated into the following consonant, while the initial hamzat al-waṣl is omitted.

f: Why can اختصم and اقتتل produce forms such as يَخْصِم and يَقْتُل with an apparently three-letter surface form?
b: The initial hamzat al-waṣl is dropped, and the tāʾ of the افتعال pattern is assimilated into the following consonant. Thus the surface form conceals the additional morphological material present in the underlying form.

f: What is one optional pronunciation of the initial radical in verbs such as خصم and قتل after assimilation?
b: The first radical may be opened, producing خَصَم and قَتَل in the relevant pronunciation, through transferring the vowel of the assimilated consonant to the preceding consonant.

f: What alternative pronunciation of the initial radical in خصم and قتل is mentioned?
b: It may be given kasrah, producing خِصْم and قِتْل in the relevant forms. This follows the principle that when a consonant is moved after being sākin, kasrah is suitable.

f: Why is kasrah considered preferable to transferring the vowel in the pronunciation of forms such as خصم and قتل?
b: Because the first pronunciation can create ambiguity between the past of the افتعال and تفعيل patterns after deletion of the initial hamzah, whereas kasrah avoids this difficulty.

f: What further dialectal pronunciation can occur after giving kasrah to the first radical in خصم and قتل?
b: Some Arabs also give kasrah to the following radical by vowel assimilation, producing forms such as خِصِم and قِتِل in the cited dialectal usage.

f: What is the general rule for the present-tense prefix of an active present verb whose past tense has four letters?
b: Its present-tense prefix is always ḍammah, as in يدحرج، يكرم، يقاتل، يفرح.

f: What is the morphological sign distinguishing an active present verb such as يدحرج from its passive counterpart?
b: In the active form, the letter immediately before the final radical is always kasrah. In the passive, that position is given fatḥah.

f: What is the active present conjugation of نصر in the third-person masculine?
b: ينصر، ينصران، ينصرون: masculine singular, dual, and plural.

f: What is the active present conjugation of نصر in the third-person feminine?
b: تنصر، تنصران، ينصرن: feminine singular, dual, and plural.

f: What is the active present conjugation of نصر in the second-person masculine?
b: تنصر، تنصران، تنصرون: masculine singular, dual, and plural.

f: What is the active present conjugation of نصر in the second-person feminine?
b: تنصرين، تنصران، تنصرن: feminine singular, dual, and plural.

f: What is the active present conjugation of نصر in the first person?
b: أنصر for the first-person singular and ننصر for the first-person plural.

f: What is the complete active present-tense conjugation of نصر?
b: ينصر، ينصران، ينصرون؛ تنصر، تنصران، ينصرن؛ تنصر، تنصران، تنصرون؛ تنصرين، تنصران، تنصرن؛ أنصر، ننصر.

f: Can a dual form in Arabic sometimes be used to address or refer to a single person?
b: Yes. The author cites poetic examples in which a dual form is used for a single person, such as فإن تزجراني يا ابن عفان أنزجر.

f: What poetic example does the author give of a dual form being used for a single person?
b: فإن تزجراني يا ابن عفان أنزجر وإن تدعاني أحم عرضًا ممنعًا. The dual forms تزجراني and تدعاني refer to a single person in the cited usage.

f: What second poetic example does the author give of a dual form being used for a single person?
b: فقلت لصاحبي لا تخبسانا بنزع أصول واجتزاز شيحًا. The dual form is used in addressing a single companion.

f: Which active present-tense verb patterns does the author say can be conjugated by analogy with ينصر?
b: Examples include يضرب، يعلم، يدحرج، يكرم، يقاتل، يفرح، يتكسر، يتباعد، ينقطع، يجتمع، يحمر، يحمار، يستخرج، يعشوشب، يقعنسس، يسلنقى، يجلوذ، يتدحرج، يحرنجم، ويقشعر.

f: Why does the author not provide a detailed conjugation of every active present-tense pattern?
b: Because the same conjugational procedure applies throughout, and a student with even basic discrimination should be able to infer the remaining forms. Even forms such as يقشعر and يسلنقى can be understood by applying the established rules concerning doubled and defective verbs.

f: How should an active present-tense verb with a basic triliteral past such as نصر normally begin?
b: Its present-tense prefix is normally opened with fatḥah, as in يَنصر، تَنصر، أَنصر، نَنصر.

f: How should an active present-tense verb derived from a four-letter past such as دحرج begin?
b: Its present-tense prefix is ḍammah, as in يُدحرج.

f: How should the active present-tense forms of أكرم and قاتل begin?
b: They begin with a ḍammah on the present-tense prefix: يُكرم and يُقاتل.

f: How should the active present-tense form of فرح begin?
b: It begins with a ḍammah on the present-tense prefix: يَفرح in the standard three-letter classification discussed here.

f: What is the distinction between the active present forms يَفعل and يُفعل with respect to the number of letters in their corresponding past forms?
b: يَفعل generally corresponds to a past tense with three letters, while يُفعل corresponds to a past tense with four letters, such as أكرم → يُكرم.

f: Why does the author say that the letter immediately before the final radical is always kasrah in the active present forms of four-letter past verbs?
b: This kasrah is the morphological sign distinguishing the active form from the passive, in which the corresponding position is given fatḥah.

f: What is the morphological sign of the passive present tense (المضارع المبني للمفعول)?
b: Its present-tense prefix is ḍammah, and the letter immediately before the final radical is fatḥah.

f: What is the vowel of the letter immediately before the final radical in an Arabic passive present verb?
b: It is always fatḥah, as in يُنصر، يُدحرج، يُكرم، يُقاتل، يُفرح، يُستخرج.

f: What is the difference between the active and passive present forms of نصر?
b: The active is يَنصر, with fatḥah on the present-tense prefix and ḍammah on the letter before the final radical; the passive is يُنصر, with ḍammah on the prefix and fatḥah before the final radical.

f: What is the difference between the active and passive present forms of دحرج?
b: The active is يُدحرج and the passive is يُدحرج in the relevant vocalization distinction: the active has kasrah on the letter before the final radical (يُدحرِج), while the passive has fatḥah there (يُدحرَج).

f: What is the difference between the active and passive present forms of أكرم?
b: The active is يُكرِم and the passive is يُكرَم. Both have ḍammah on the present-tense prefix, but the active has kasrah before the final radical while the passive has fatḥah.

f: What is the difference between the active and passive present forms of قاتل?
b: The active is يُقاتِل and the passive is يُقاتَل. The present-tense prefix is ḍammah in both, while the active has kasrah and the passive fatḥah before the final radical.

f: What is the difference between the active and passive present forms of استخرج?
