b: Their underlying morphological structures consist entirely of weak letters. The passage analyzes ياء as being composed of three yāʾs originally, while واو is analyzed according to differing views concerning the origin of its alif.

f: Why are the names of letters such as أ، ب، ج considered names rather than the letters themselves?
b: Saying ألف، باء، جيم refers to the names assigned to the letters, just as “man” and “horse” are names of their referents. The actual thing being referred to is the letter itself, not merely its name.

f: What story does al-Khalīl tell about the word جيم?
b: Al-Khalīl asked his students how they pronounced the jīm in جعفر. They answered جيم, and he pointed out that they had pronounced the name of the letter rather than the actual letter being asked about. The proper answer, referring to the letter itself, would be ج.

f: How is ياء analyzed morphologically?
b: It is analyzed as consisting of three yāʾs, i.e. ييي, according to the agreement mentioned in the passage. The final yāʾ is changed into hamzah as a form of phonetic lightening, while the middle yāʾ changes into alif.

f: How can the form ياء be derived from the underlying ييي?
b: One analysis changes the final yāʾ into hamzah for lightening, producing ييء, and then changes the middle yāʾ into alif because it is moving and preceded by fatḥah, yielding ياء. Another description performs the middle-yāʾ → alif change first and then the final-yāʾ → hamzah change.

f: Where does the alif of واو come from?
b: Al-Akhfash held that the alif is derived from the original wāw. Another opinion derives it from yāʾ, but the first view is considered stronger because wāw-initial words are more numerous than yāʾ-initial ones, making the wāw origin more likely.

f: Why is the middle weak letter of واو changed into alif rather than the final one?
b: This avoids the undesirable combination of two consecutive moving weak letters at the beginning of the word. The middle weak letter is therefore the one converted to alif.

f: What chapter begins after the discussion of the seven types of weak verbs?
b: The chapter فصل في المهموز begins. It discusses verbs whose root contains a hamzah.

f: What is a مهموز verb?
b: A مهموز verb is one in which one of the original root letters is hamzah.

f: How many types of مهموز verbs are there?
b: There are three types, according to the position of the hamzah: مهموز الفاء (hamzated first radical), مهموز العين (hamzated middle radical), and مهموز اللام (hamzated final radical).

f: What alternative names are given for the three types of مهموز?
b: مهموز الفاء is also called مهموز الصدر, مهموز العين is called مهموز الأوسط, and مهموز اللام is called مهموز العجز.

f: What is the basic morphological rule governing a hamzated verb?
b: A hamzated verb is generally conjugated like a sound verb, because hamzah is a consonant rather than one of the weak letters.

f: Does saying that a مهموز verb follows the rules of a sound verb mean that every hamzated verb is treated identically?
b: No. More precisely, a hamzated verb follows the rules of its corresponding non-hamzated category. Thus a hamzated doubled verb behaves like a doubled verb, a hamzated mithāl like a mithāl, a hamzated hollow verb like a hollow verb, and so forth.

f: Why is مهموز classified among the non-sound verbs?
b: Although hamzah is a strong consonant, it frequently undergoes special changes such as substitution with weak letters, deletion, or phonetic easing, which do not normally affect fully sound roots.

f: What is the relationship between hamzah and weak letters?
b: Hamzah can sometimes be changed into a weak letter, which is one reason hamzated verbs receive separate treatment from completely sound verbs.

f: When is hamzah particularly susceptible to easing?
b: Hamzah is especially subject to easing when it occurs after something has already preceded it, i.e. when it is not the first sound of the utterance.

f: Why is hamzah normally retained when it begins an utterance?
b: Beginning a word with a strong consonant is preferred. Hamzah is a strong consonant from the far end of the throat, so it is not normally weakened when it is the initial sound.

f: Why can hamzah be changed when it is not at the beginning of speech?
b: Once something precedes it, the need for a strong initial consonant disappears, allowing the hamzah to undergo phonetic easing.

f: What example illustrates the easing of an initial hamzah when it is preceded by something?
b: وَأَمَرَ may be pronounced with the hamzah eased in connected speech, represented in the passage as وَامَرَ, whereas when beginning directly with the word, the hamzah is retained.

f: Why does the author emphasize that “non-initial” means non-initial in speech rather than merely non-initial in the written word?
b: A hamzah may be written at the beginning of a word but cease to be the first sound when the word is connected to something before it. The phonetic condition therefore concerns whether the hamzah begins the utterance, not merely its position within the written word.

f: Why does the author mention the need for hamzat al-waṣl when discussing hamzah easing?
b: Hamzat al-waṣl itself is supplied precisely when a word would otherwise begin with a consonant that cannot be pronounced initially. This shows that Arabic has a preference for avoiding an initial difficult or impermissible consonantal configuration.

f: Is the deletion of hamzah in خُذْ an example of ordinary hamzah easing?
b: No. خُذْ derives historically from a form such as أُؤْخُذْ, but the deletion of hamzat al-waṣl is a separate phenomenon. Hamzat al-waṣl is obligatorily dropped when it is no longer needed for pronunciation in connected speech.

f: What is the difference between hamzah easing and deletion of hamzat al-waṣl?
b: Hamzah easing is a treatment of an original hamzah, often involving substitution, deletion, or another phonetic change. Hamzat al-waṣl, by contrast, is inherently an auxiliary hamzah that is deleted when connection to a preceding word makes it unnecessary.

f: Why is hamzah sometimes eased?
b: Hamzah is a strong consonant originating from the farthest part of the throat, so easing it reduces phonetic difficulty. The passage notes that the exact forms of hamzah easing are extensive and are not fully treated in this book.

f: What are the main methods by which hamzah can be eased?
b: The passage mentions replacement (القلب), deletion (الحذف), and other forms of phonetic treatment. A complete discussion would require a much longer treatment.

f: How does the verb أَمَلَ يَأْمَلُ behave?
b: It follows the pattern of نصر ينصر in its regular conjugation because the hamzah is treated like a sound radical.

f: What is the imperative of أَمَلَ يَأْمَلُ?
b: The imperative is أَوْمِلْ, with the hamzah of the root changed into wāw.

f: Why is the imperative of أمل pronounced أومل?
b: The original imperative would contain two hamzahs, the first being hamzat al-waṣl and the second being the hamzated fāʾ of the root. The second hamzah is sākin, so it is changed into wāw because the preceding hamzah carries a ḍammah.

f: What is the underlying form of the imperative أومل?
b: Its underlying form is أُؤْمِلْ: the first hamzah is hamzat al-waṣl and the second hamzah is the original fāʾ of the verb.

f: What happens when two hamzahs meet in one word and the second hamzah is sākin?
b: The second, sākin hamzah is obligatorily changed into a weak letter corresponding to the vowel of the preceding hamzah. With a preceding ḍammah, it becomes wāw.

f: Why is the second hamzah in أُؤْمِلْ changed into wāw?
b: Because the second hamzah is sākin and the preceding hamzah has ḍammah. For ease of pronunciation, the sākin hamzah takes the corresponding weak letter, wāw, yielding أَوْمِلْ.

f: What is the general principle behind changing a sākin hamzah after a preceding vowel?
b: When two hamzahs occur together in one word and the second is sākin, the second hamzah is changed into the weak letter corresponding to the movement of the preceding hamzah: ḍammah → wāw, with the other corresponding changes governed by the relevant vowel.

f: What is meant by the statement “ثانيتهما ساكنة” in the rule for two hamzahs?
b: It means that when two hamzahs occur together in one word, the second hamzah is sākin. The phrase is a circumstantial clause describing the condition of the second hamzah.

f: What happens when two hamzahs occur together in one word and the second hamzah is sākin?
b: The second hamzah is changed into the weak letter corresponding to the vowel of the first hamzah, in order to lighten pronunciation.

f: What does a sākin second hamzah become when the first hamzah has fatḥah?
b: It becomes alif, because alif corresponds to fatḥah. For example, آمَنَ derives from أَأْمَنَ, with the second hamzah changed into alif.

f: What does a sākin second hamzah become when the first hamzah has ḍammah?
b: It becomes wāw, because wāw corresponds to ḍammah. For example, أُومِنَ derives from أُؤْمِنَ by changing the second sākin hamzah into wāw.

f: What does a sākin second hamzah become when the first hamzah has kasrah?
b: It becomes yāʾ, because yāʾ corresponds to kasrah. The passage gives إِيمَان as an example of this type of hamzah transformation.

f: Why does the rule specify that the two hamzahs must occur in “one word”?
b: When the two hamzahs occur in separate words, they can be separated by a word boundary, so changing the second hamzah is not obligatory. It may nevertheless be permissible in some cases.

f: What example demonstrates that two hamzahs in separate words do not have to undergo the same obligatory change?
b: The passage gives يا قارئ ائزر, where the hamzahs may be pronounced as hamzahs, although pronunciation with a wāw is also permissible according to the discussion.

f: Does every sākin hamzah have to change into alif, wāw, or yāʾ according to the preceding vowel?
b: No. A sākin hamzah preceded by an ordinary consonant does not have to undergo this change. For example, رَأْس، بُؤْس، رِئْم may retain their hamzah, although easing can be permissible.

f: Why does the author specifically mention that the second hamzah is sākin?
b: Because a second hamzah that is moving has different rules. The particular rule being discussed concerns two hamzahs in one word where the second is sākin.

f: What happens when two hamzahs occur in one word but the second hamzah is moving?
b: The specific rule of obligatorily changing the second hamzah into alif, wāw, or yāʾ does not apply. A different set of hamzah rules governs the form.

f: What apparent exception to the rule of changing the second sākin hamzah is mentioned?
b: The word أَيِّمَة is mentioned. Its underlying form is analyzed as containing two hamzahs, yet the second hamzah is not changed into alif as the general rule would predict.

f: How does the commentator explain the apparent exception of أَيِّمَة?
b: He can answer the objection by treating أَيِّمَة as a shādh (irregular/non-analogical) form, so it does not invalidate the general rule.

f: What happens to a wāw or yāʾ that resulted from changing a second hamzah when hamzat al-waṣl is dropped in connected speech?
b: The substituted wāw or yāʾ returns to the original hamzah.

f: Why does the substituted wāw or yāʾ return to hamzah when hamzat al-waṣl is dropped?
b: The original substitution occurred because two hamzahs met in one word. When hamzat al-waṣl is dropped in connected speech, the two hamzahs no longer meet, so the reason for changing the second hamzah disappears. The original hamzah therefore returns.

f: What does “عند الوصل” mean in the discussion of restoring an original hamzah?
b: Here الوصل means connecting the word to what precedes it, so that its hamzat al-waṣl is no longer pronounced. It does not simply mean continuous pronunciation in general.

f: Does the original hamzah return only when the letter before the second hamzah has fatḥah?
b: No. The commentator explicitly rejects this restriction. The original hamzah returns whenever the hamzat al-waṣl disappears, whether the preceding vowel is fatḥah, ḍammah, or kasrah.

f: Why does the commentator reject restricting hamzah restoration to a preceding fatḥah?
b: Because the actual cause of the original hamzah changing was the meeting of two hamzahs. Once hamzat al-waṣl disappears, that meeting is removed regardless of whether the preceding vowel is fatḥah, ḍammah, or kasrah.

f: What Qurʾānic example illustrates restoration of a yāʾ-derived hamzah when hamzat al-waṣl disappears after a fatḥah?
b: The passage cites إلى الهدى ائتنا, whose relevant underlying form contains the original hamzah. When hamzat al-waṣl is dropped in connected speech, the original hamzah returns.

f: What Qurʾānic example illustrates restoration of a yāʾ-derived hamzah when hamzat al-waṣl disappears after a ḍammah?
b: The passage cites فمنهم من يقول ائذن له. When the initial hamzat al-waṣl of the relevant form drops, the original hamzah is restored.

f: What Qurʾānic example illustrates restoration of a wāw-derived hamzah when hamzat al-waṣl disappears after a kasrah?
b: The passage cites والذي اؤتمن أمانته. When the initial hamzat al-waṣl drops, the original hamzah returns rather than remaining represented by the substituted weak letter.

f: What happens to the wāw in أومل when the word is connected to a preceding word?
b: The wāw, which arose by changing the second hamzah of أُؤْمِلْ, returns to the original hamzah when hamzat al-waṣl drops in connected speech.

f: How does the restoration principle apply to the imperative ائملي?
b: When the initial hamzat al-waṣl drops in connected speech, the substituted yāʾ returns to the original hamzah, because the two-hamzah environment that caused the substitution no longer exists.

f: Why is the substituted weak letter in forms such as أومل not considered an original root letter?
b: The wāw or yāʾ is merely a replacement for the original hamzah. It arose because of a particular phonetic environment and therefore disappears when that environment disappears.

f: What is the general rule for a sākin second hamzah following a hamzah in the same word?
b: It is changed according to the vowel of the first hamzah: fatḥah → alif, ḍammah → wāw, kasrah → yāʾ.

f: What is the general rule for restoring a hamzah that had been changed into wāw or yāʾ because of hamzat al-waṣl?
b: When hamzat al-waṣl drops in connected speech, the substituted wāw or yāʾ returns to the original hamzah because the meeting of the two hamzahs has disappeared.

f: Why is the substitution of the second hamzah considered a form of phonetic easing?
b: Hamzah is a strong consonant, and pronouncing two hamzahs together—especially when the second is sākin—is heavy. Replacing the second hamzah with alif, wāw, or yāʾ makes pronunciation easier.

f: What is the key distinction between hamzah substitution and hamzat al-waṣl deletion?
b: Hamzah substitution changes an original hamzah into a corresponding weak letter because of phonetic difficulty. Hamzat al-waṣl deletion removes an auxiliary hamzah when it is no longer needed to permit pronunciation at the beginning of a word.

f: Why does the disappearance of hamzat al-waṣl remove the reason for hamzah substitution?
b: With hamzat al-waṣl pronounced, there are effectively two consecutive hamzahs, creating the phonetic difficulty that triggers substitution. Once hamzat al-waṣl is dropped in connected speech, only the original hamzah remains, so substitution is no longer necessary.

f: Why are the original hamzahs omitted in the imperative forms خُذْ, كُلْ, and مُرْ?
b: The omission is non-analogical (شاذ) and is attributed to the frequency of usage of these words.

f: What would the regular analogical imperative forms of خُذْ, كُلْ, and مُرْ be if their original hamzahs were retained?
b: Their expected forms would be أُؤْخُذْ, أُؤْكُلْ, and أُؤْمُرْ, by analogy with forms such as أُؤْمَلْ from تَأَمَّلَ.

f: Why do the forms خُذْ, كُلْ, and مُرْ contain two deleted hamzahs?
b: When forming these imperatives, the original hamzah of the verb was first deleted because of the frequency of these forms. The hamzat al-waṣl was then also deleted because it was no longer needed once the word was connected in speech and no longer began with a consonant requiring it.

f: Is the deletion in خُذْ, كُلْ, and مُرْ completely identical in all three words?
b: Not precisely. The author groups the three together for convenience, but خُذْ and كُلْ have obligatory deletion, whereas مُرْ can also occur in its original form and is therefore not identical in this respect.

f: Why can مُرْ sometimes retain its original hamzah in connected speech?
b: Because when the hamzat al-waṣl is omitted in connected speech, the phonetic heaviness that originally motivated the deletion is removed. Thus مُرْ may occur as وَأْمُرْ in the Qurʾānic expression وَأْمُرْ أَهْلَكَ بِالصَّلَاةِ.

f: Why is وَأْمُرْ considered more eloquent than وَمُرْ in the cited Qurʾānic context?
b: وَأْمُرْ preserves the original hamzah after the hamzat al-waṣl has been dropped. The removal of hamzat al-waṣl eliminates the phonetic heaviness caused by the two hamzahs, so there is no longer a reason to retain the shortened form مُرْ.

f: What hadith evidence is cited for the occurrence of the original form مُرْ with its hamzah restored?
b: The passage cites expressions such as فَمُرْ بالستر and فَمُرْ بالكلب, demonstrating that the original form can occur in connected speech.

f: What is the general rule illustrated by the imperatives أَيْزِرْ, أُودِبْ, and اسْأَلْ?
b: Hamzated verbs normally follow the rules of their corresponding sound verbs, while the hamzah may undergo specific phonetic changes when two hamzahs meet or when frequent usage produces an irregular shortened form.

f: What is the imperative of تَأَزَّرَ according to the regular rule?
b: The imperative is ائْزِرْ, analogous to a regular imperative such as اضْرِبْ. The second hamzah changes into yāʾ because it is sākin and follows a hamzah with kasrah.

f: Why is the imperative of تَأَزَّرَ written ائْزِرْ?
b: Its underlying form contains two hamzahs, ائْزِرْ being derived from the relevant hamzated structure. The second hamzah is changed into yāʾ because it is sākin and follows a hamzah with kasrah.

f: Why does the author specifically mention أَيْزِرْ as an example?
b: It demonstrates the conversion of a second hamzah into yāʾ after kasrah, a change that is not present in the otherwise similar example اهنئ.

f: What is the imperative of أَدَّبَ or the relevant hamzated verb يَأْدَبُ?
b: The imperative is أَوْدِبْ, derived from an underlying form with two hamzahs, with the second hamzah changed into wāw.

f: Why does the second hamzah in أُؤْدِبْ become wāw?
b: The second hamzah is sākin and follows a hamzah carrying ḍammah, so it changes into wāw, the weak letter corresponding to ḍammah.

f: What is the regular imperative of سَأَلَ يَسْأَلُ?
b: The regular imperative is اسْأَلْ, analogous to the imperative امْنَعْ from يَمْنَعُ.

f: What shortened imperative of سَأَلَ is also permitted?
b: سَلْ is also permitted. It results from further hamzah reduction and deletion of the resulting alif because of the meeting of two sukūns.

f: How is the shortened imperative سَلْ related to the imperative اسْأَلْ?
b: سَلْ is an irregularly shortened form of اسْأَلْ. The second hamzah may be changed into alif, producing a form equivalent to سال, after which the unnecessary hamzat al-waṣl is omitted and the alif is deleted because of two consecutive sukūns.

f: What Qurʾānic reading preserves the alif in the form سال سائل?
b: The passage cites the reading سَالَ سَائِلٌ, which preserves the alif resulting from the hamzah transformation.

f: Is the transformation producing سَلْ from سَأَلْ a regular productive rule?
b: No. The passage explicitly treats it as not a continuously applicable analogical rule. It is an attested form associated with particular usage.

f: Why is the imperative سَلْ able to dispense with hamzat al-waṣl?
b: Once the original hamzah has been changed into alif and the relevant vowel/consonant changes have occurred, the form no longer requires hamzat al-waṣl in the same way. The resulting alif is then deleted because of the meeting of two sukūns, yielding سَلْ.

f: How do some grammarians classify سَأَلَ يَسْأَلُ morphologically?
b: Some grammarians classify it as hollow wāwī, analogous to خَافَ يَخَافُ, while others classify it as hollow yāʾī, analogous to هَابَ يَهَابُ.

f: Why might one object to deleting the hamzat al-waṣl from سَلْ?
b: One could argue that the vowel on the sīn is merely incidental, so it should perhaps not prevent recognition of the need for hamzat al-waṣl, just as in certain forms such as اجْأَرْ and آرْأَفْ, where the hamzat al-waṣl is retained despite the preceding consonant receiving an incidental vowel.

f: How does the passage answer the objection concerning the deletion of hamzat al-waṣl in سَلْ?
b: It answers that سَلْ is much more frequently used, so greater phonetic shortening is tolerated in this highly frequent form.

f: What alternative explanation does the passage give for the form سَلْ?
b: It can be derived directly from تَسْأَلُ: the present-tense prefix is removed, the remaining form is made appropriate for the imperative, and the alif is subsequently deleted because it meets another sākin. This derivation differs from forms such as اجْأَرْ and آرْأَفْ, whose shortening occurs only in the imperative.

f: What does آبَ يَؤُوبُ mean?
b: آبَ يَؤُوبُ means “he returned” or “he came back.”

f: What is the morphological pattern of آبَ يَؤُوبُ?
b: It follows the same general pattern as a hollow verb such as صَانَ يَصُونُ.

f: What does سَاءَ يَسُوءُ mean?
b: سَاءَ يَسُوءُ means “he/it was bad, harmed, or displeased,” depending on the context.

f: What does جَاءَ يَجِيءُ mean?
b: جَاءَ يَجِيءُ means “he came.”

f: Why does the passage mention the forms سَاءَ and جَاءَ specifically?
b: Their active participles are سَاءٍ and جَاءٍ, and their morphological derivation involves a particular discussion about how the original weak letters and hamzahs underwent transformation.

f: What is the active participle of سَاءَ according to the passage?
b: The active participle is سَاءٍ.

f: What is the active participle of جَاءَ according to the passage?
b: The active participle is جَاءٍ.

f: Why are سَاءٍ and جَاءٍ not treated simply like صَائِن and بَائِع?
b: Their derivation involves additional hamzah transformations, so their historical and morphological analysis is more complicated than the ordinary hollow-verb examples صَائِن and بَائِع.

f: What is Sībawayh's analysis of the origin of سَاءَ and جَاءَ?
b: Sībawayh analyzes them as ultimately derived from forms such as سَاوَى and جَايَأَ/جَايَى in which weak letters underwent transformation into hamzah and further changes.

f: According to Sībawayh, what happens in the derivation of سَاءَ and جَاءَ?
b: According to the analysis presented, the original form undergoes several changes: a weak letter is changed into hamzah, producing a form with two hamzahs; the second hamzah then changes into yāʾ because of the preceding kasrah; further weak-letter changes eventually produce سَاءَ and جَاءَ.

f: Why does Sībawayh's analysis of سَاءَ and جَاءَ involve two hamzahs?
b: His derivation produces an intermediate form containing two consecutive hamzahs, and the phonetic rules governing the meeting of two hamzahs then require further transformation.

f: How does the analysis of سَاءَ and جَاءَ eventually produce the forms with a single hamzah?
b: After the intermediate transformations produce forms such as سَائِي and جَائِي, further application of the same type of weak-letter treatment found in forms such as غازٍ and رامٍ produces سَاءٍ and جَاءٍ.

f: What morphological pattern does Sībawayh assign to سَاءَ and جَاءَ?
b: He analyzes their resulting pattern as فَاعٍ in the relevant morphological discussion.

f: What is al-Khalīl's analysis of the origin of سَاءَ and جَاءَ?
b: Al-Khalīl gives a different analysis: the original letters exchange positions, with the ʿayn moved to the position of the lām and the lām moved to the position of the ʿayn, producing forms such as سَاءَوْ and جَاءَيْ before further weak-letter changes.

f: What morphological pattern does al-Khalīl assign to the intermediate forms سَاءَوْ and جَاءَيْ?
b: Al-Khalīl analyzes the intermediate forms as being on the pattern فَالَع.

f: What further transformation does al-Khalīl apply to the intermediate forms سَاءَوْ and جَاءَيْ?
b: He applies the same type of final-weak transformation used in forms such as غازٍ and رامٍ, eventually yielding سَاءَ and جَاءَ.

f: Why does the passage prefer al-Khalīl's analysis of سَاءَ and جَاءَ over Sībawayh's analysis?
b: The passage prefers al-Khalīl because his analysis requires fewer changes. Sībawayh's analysis requires two additional transformations: changing the ʿayn into hamzah and changing the lām into yāʾ.

f: Why does the passage say that al-Khalīl's analysis involves fewer changes?
b: Al-Khalīl directly rearranges the original weak letters and then applies the necessary weak-letter transformation, whereas Sībawayh introduces additional hamzah and yāʾ substitutions before reaching the final form.

f: What examples demonstrate that Arabic can change weak letters into hamzah even when doing so is not strictly necessary?
b: The passage mentions forms such as شَاكٍ from an original form containing wāw/yāʾ, نَاءَ يَنَاءُ from نَأَى يَنْأَى, and أَيْسَ from يَئِسَ. These demonstrate that such letter changes are attested in Arabic.

f: Why does the passage consider hamzah substitution especially relevant in the analysis of سَاءَ and جَاءَ?
b: Because in the proposed underlying forms, the occurrence of two hamzahs creates an actual phonetic need for transformation. Thus the hamzah changes are not merely arbitrary substitutions.

f: What did Ibn al-Ḥājib say about Sībawayh's and al-Khalīl's analyses of سَاءَ and جَاءَ?
b: Ibn al-Ḥājib considered Sībawayh's analysis more consistent with analogy, while arguing that al-Khalīl's proposed rearrangement lacks sufficient evidence.

f: Why did Ibn al-Ḥājib consider Sībawayh's analysis more analogical?
b: He regarded Sībawayh's derivation as more consistent with the established patterns of Arabic morphological behavior, whereas he did not consider al-Khalīl's letter transposition sufficiently supported by evidence.

f: What does Ibn al-Ḥājib say about the claim that letter substitution itself is analogical?
b: He argues that letter substitution (القلب) is not itself a consistently productive analogical rule in the relevant cases, so it cannot simply be assumed whenever it would produce a desired derivation.

f: What does أَسَا يَأْسُو mean?
b: أَسَا يَأْسُو means “he treated/healed”, particularly in the sense of treating an injury or ailment.

f: What is the morphological analogy for أَسَا يَأْسُو?
b: It follows the pattern of دَعَا يَدْعُو, a final-weak wāwī verb.

f: What does أَتَى يَأْتِي mean?
b: أَتَى يَأْتِي means “he came,” “he arrived,” or “he brought,” depending on its syntactic and semantic context.

f: What is the morphological analogy for أَتَى يَأْتِي?
b: It follows the pattern of a final-weak yāʾī verb such as رَمَى يَرْمِي.

f: What is the imperative of أَتَى يَأْتِي?
b: The imperative is إِيتِ.

f: What is the underlying form of the imperative إِيتِ?
b: Its underlying form is ائْتِ. The second hamzah is changed into yāʾ because it is sākin and follows a hamzah with kasrah, just as in إِيمَان.

f: Why is the imperative إِيتِ specifically mentioned in the discussion of أَتَى يَأْتِي?
b: It illustrates the rule whereby the second of two hamzahs is changed into yāʾ when it is sākin and preceded by a hamzah carrying kasrah.

f: What alternative imperative form of أَتَى يَأْتِي do some Arabs use?
b: Some Arabs say تِ for the imperative, analogous to خُذْ.

f: How is the alternative imperative تِ derived?
b: According to this dialect, the second hamzah of the underlying ائْتِ is deleted, after which hamzat al-waṣl is no longer needed, leaving تِ.

f: What happens to the alternative imperative تِ when it occurs in pause?
b: In pause, it becomes تِهْ, with hāʾ al-sakt, analogous to قِهْ from قِ.

f: Why is the alternative imperative تِ compared to خُذْ?
b: Both are examples of highly shortened imperatives in which hamzah is deleted beyond the normal analogical rule because of frequent usage.

f: What is the meaning and morphological pattern of وَأَى يَئِي?
b: وَأَى يَئِي means “he promised” and follows the same general pattern as وَقَى يَقِي.

f: What is the underlying form of يَئِي in وَأَى يَئِي?
b: Its underlying form is يُوْئِي

f: Why does the author compare وَأَى يَئِي with وَقَى يَقِي?
b: Both verbs have an initial weak wāw that undergoes deletion in the present tense, so their morphological treatment is analogous.

f: What is the meaning and morphological pattern of أَوَى يَأْوِي?
b: أَوَى يَأْوِي means “he took refuge, sheltered, or resorted to” and follows the pattern of شَوَى يَشْوِي.

f: What is the underlying form of the maṣdar أَيًّا in the discussion of أَوَى يَأْوِي?
b: The passage analyzes it as originally أَوْيًا, with the relevant weak-letter changes producing the cited form.

f: Why does the author mention the maṣdar of أَوَى يَأْوِي even though the maṣdar itself adds no new morphological rule?
b: The commentator explains that its purpose is to indicate that the maṣdar undergoes the same type of weak-letter treatment as the analogous verb شَوَى يَشْوِي, even though the maṣdar is not normally included among the تصاريف being listed.

f: What is the imperative of أَوَى يَأْوِي?
b: The imperative is إِيوِ.

f: What is the underlying form of the imperative إِيوِ from أَوَى يَأْوِي?
b: Its underlying form is ائْوِ. The second hamzah is changed into yāʾ because it is sākin and follows a hamzah with kasrah.

f: Why is the imperative إِيوِ specifically mentioned in the discussion of أَوَى يَأْوِي?
b: It illustrates an additional hamzah transformation: the second hamzah of ائْوِ becomes yāʾ, just as in إِيتِ and إِيمَان.

f: What happens to the yāʾ in forms such as إِيتِ, إِيزِرْ, and إِيوِ when hamzat al-waṣl disappears in connected speech?
b: The yāʾ returns to its original hamzah when hamzat al-waṣl drops in connected speech, because the meeting of the two hamzahs that caused the substitution no longer exists.

f: What Qurʾānic example demonstrates the restoration of an original hamzah after hamzat al-waṣl disappears in connected speech?
b: The passage cites فَأَوَوْا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ. The underlying imperative is analyzed as ائْوُوا, with two hamzahs and two wāws. When the preceding فَـ causes hamzat al-waṣl to drop, the original hamzah returns, giving فَأَوَوْا.

f: How is the form فَأَوَوْا derived according to the passage?
b: The underlying form is ائْوُوا. The second hamzah is changed into a weak letter under the two-hamzah rule. When the form is connected to فَـ, hamzat al-waṣl drops, the original hamzah returns, and the resulting form is فَأَوَوْا.

f: What does نَأَى يَنْأَى mean?
b: نَأَى يَنْأَى means “he moved away,” “he became distant,” or “he was far away.”

f: What is the morphological analogy for نَأَى يَنْأَى?
b: It follows the pattern of a final-weak verb such as رَعَى يَرْعَى.

f: What is the regular expected present-tense form of رَأَى if it followed the pattern of نَأَى and رَعَى?
b: The expected form would be يَرْأَى, analogous to يَنْأَى and يَرْعَى.

f: Why does رَأَى يَرَى not retain the hamzah in its present tense?
b: The Arabs are unanimously reported to have deleted the ʿayn radical hamzah from its present tense because of the frequency of the verb and the resulting ease of pronunciation.

f: Why does the author say that the hamzah is deleted “from its present tense” in the discussion of رَأَى?
b: The wording is intended to establish that the deletion applies to the present-tense paradigm generally, rather than being restricted only to the particular form يَرَى.

f: What is the full present-tense conjugation of رَأَى after the deletion of its ʿayn hamzah?
b: يَرَى، يَرَيَانِ، يَرَوْنَ؛ تَرَى، تَرَيَانِ، يَرَيْنَ؛ تَرَى، تَرَيَانِ، تَرَوْنَ؛ تَرَيْنَ، تَرَيَانِ، تَرَيْنَ؛ أَرَى، نَرَى.

f: What is the underlying form of يَرَى before the hamzah is deleted?
b: Its underlying form is يَرْأَى

f: What two operations produce يَرَى from the underlying hamzated form?
b: First, the movement of the hamzah is transferred to the preceding letter; second, the hamzah itself is deleted. The result is يَرَى.

f: Is the deletion of the hamzah from يَرَى merely an optional pronunciation?
b: No. The deletion is described as obligatory in normal usage because of the verb's high frequency. The form يَرْأَى is not normally used except in poetic necessity.

f: Why is the hamzah deletion in يَرَى considered non-analogical?
b: It is a special lexical shortening caused by the frequency of usage of رَأَى. It is therefore not a general rule that permits the hamzah to be deleted from every verb with a similar structure.

f: Can the form يَرْأَى ever occur?
b: Yes, but only exceptionally, particularly in poetic necessity. Normal Arabic uses يَرَى.

f: How does the treatment of رَأَى يَرَى differ from the regular treatment of نَأَى يَنْأَى?
b: نَأَى يَنْأَى retains its ʿayn hamzah according to the normal pattern, whereas رَأَى يَرَى undergoes a special, obligatory deletion of the ʿayn hamzah because of its exceptionally frequent usage.

f: What broader principle does the discussion of إِيتِ, إِيوِ, and يَرَى illustrate?
b: Hamzated verbs generally follow the normal rules of Arabic morphology, but frequent usage can produce additional, non-analogical shortening, including deletion of hamzah.

f: What should be kept in mind when studying these hamzated and weak verbs?
b: Their rules should be compared with the previously discussed rules of weak verbs, hamzah transformation, and nūn al-tawkīd. Once those earlier rules are mastered, the apparently complicated forms can be derived systematically rather than memorized individually.

f: What poetic evidence is cited for the non-analogical deletion of the hamzah in the present tense of رَأَى?
b: The passage cites the line أَلَمْ تَرَ مَا أَلْقَيْتُ وَالدَّهْرُ أَعْصُرٌ ۝ وَمَنْ يَتَمَلَّ الْعَيْشَ يَرَأْ وَيَسْمَعْ, in which يَرَأْ retains the hamzah, even though the normal form is يَرَ.

f: What does the poetic form يَرَأْ demonstrate about the present tense of رَأَى?
b: It demonstrates that although ordinary Arabic uses يَرَى with deletion of the hamzah, the hamzah can exceptionally be retained in poetry.

f: What is the normal grammatical form corresponding to the poetic form يَرَأْ?
b: The normal form is يَرَى.

f: What additional poetic evidence is cited for retaining the hamzah in the present tense of رَأَى?
b: The passage cites the line أَرَى عَيْنِي مَا لَمْ تَرَايَا in which the poet preserves the hamzah-related form in a poetic context.

f: What poetic evidence demonstrates that the hamzah can also be deleted from the past tense of رَأَى?
b: The poet says صَاحِ هَلْ رَيْتَ أَوْ سَمِعْتَ بِرَاعٍ. The form رَيْتَ is an exceptional shortened form of the normal رَأَيْتَ.

f: What is the normal form corresponding to the poetic رَيْتَ?
b: The normal form is رَأَيْتَ.

f: Why is hamzah deletion not obligatory in a verb such as يَنْأَى?
b: Because يَنْأَى did not reach the exceptionally high frequency of يَرَى. The deletion of the hamzah in يَرَى is therefore a special shortening caused by frequent usage and does not extend automatically to other verbs.

f: What happens to the forms of رَأَى when addressing a feminine singular and a feminine plural?
b: The surface form is the same: تَرَيْنَ can mean either “you (one woman) see” or “you (women) see.” However, their underlying morphological weights are different.

f: What is the morphological weight of the feminine singular form تَرَيْنَ from رَأَى?
b: Its weight is تَفْعِينَ. It derives from تَرْأَيِينَ: the hamzah is deleted, producing تَرَيِّينَ, and subsequent weak-letter changes result in تَرَيْنَ, with both the ʿayn and lām positions undergoing deletion.

f: What is the morphological weight of the feminine plural form تَرَيْنَ from رَأَى?
b: Its weight is تَفْعَلْنَ. It derives from تَرْأَيْنَ; after deletion of the hamzah, the resulting form is تَرَيْنَ, while the original fāʾ and lām positions remain represented.

f: Why do the feminine singular and feminine plural forms of رَأَى both appear as تَرَيْنَ?
b: Their surface forms coincide, but their underlying morphological structures differ. The feminine singular undergoes deletion of both the ʿayn and lām positions, whereas the feminine plural undergoes deletion of only the ʿayn hamzah.

f: What is the underlying form of the feminine singular تَرَيْنَ from رَأَى?
b: Its underlying form is تَرْأَيِينَ. The hamzah is deleted, and subsequent changes eliminate the relevant weak-letter position, producing تَرَيْنَ.

f: What is the underlying form of the feminine plural تَرَيْنَ from رَأَى?
b: Its underlying form is تَرْأَيْنَ. After deletion of the ʿayn hamzah, it becomes تَرَيْنَ, with the lām yāʾ remaining.

f: What is the key morphological difference between تَرَيْنَ meaning “you, one woman, see” and تَرَيْنَ meaning “you, women, see”?
b: In the feminine singular, the form is on the weight تَفْعِينَ and contains the feminine singular subject suffix ـينَ. In the feminine plural, it is on the weight تَفْعَلْنَ and contains the feminine plural subject marker ـنَ.

f: What is the regular imperative of رَأَى according to the original, non-shortened form?
b: The imperative is ارْأَ according to the original morphological analysis, analogous to ارْعَ.

f: How is the imperative ارْأَ derived from رَأَى?
b: It is derived from the present تَرْأَى by deleting the present-tense prefix and the final weak radical, then adding hamzat al-waṣl with kasrah, producing ارْأَ.

f: Why is the imperative ارْأَ compared with ارْعَ?
b: Both are formed from final-weak verbs by deleting the present prefix and applying the rules governing the final weak radical in the imperative.

f: What is the morphological conjugation of the original imperative of رَأَى?
b: Its forms follow the corresponding forms of ارْعَ: ارْأَ، ارْأَيَا، ارْأَوْا؛ ارْأَيْ، ارْأَيَا، ارْأَيْنَ.

f: What shortened imperative of رَأَى results when the hamzah is deleted?
b: The shortened form is رَ.

f: How is the shortened imperative رَ derived from رَأَى?
b: The present-tense prefix is deleted and the final weak radical is deleted according to the relevant rules, while the hamzah is also omitted because of the special shortening of رَأَى. The resulting form is رَ.

f: Why is hāʾ al-sakt required when the imperative رَ is pronounced in pause?
b: Because رَ is an extremely short form ending in a moving vowel. Hāʾ al-sakt is added in pause to permit stopping on the form, producing رَهْ.

f: What analogy is used to explain the addition of hāʾ al-sakt to the imperative رَ?
b: It is compared with قِهْ, the paused form of قِ, where hāʾ al-sakt is likewise added to facilitate pausing.

f: What are the forms of the shortened imperative رَ when addressing different persons?
b: The passage gives رَ، رَيَا، رَؤُوا؛ رَيْ، رَيَا، رَيْنَ in the relevant morphological analysis, with the underlying weak letters undergoing the appropriate changes.

f: What is the underlying form of the dual masculine imperative رَؤُوا?
b: It is analyzed as deriving from رَيْوَا/رَيْوُوا through the relevant weak-letter changes; the passage presents the form as رَؤُوا in the shortened paradigm.

f: What is the underlying form of the feminine singular imperative رَيْ?
b: It is derived from رَأْيِي

f: Why does the author say that the letter rāʾ remains fatḥah in the forms of the shortened imperative رَأَى?
b: Because there is no morphological reason to change the fatḥah of the rāʾ. The vowel remains fatḥah throughout the shortened forms.

f: What is the main distinction between the regular imperative ارْأَ and the shortened imperative رَ?
b: ارْأَ preserves the original hamzah of رَأَى and follows the normal morphological derivation, whereas رَ reflects the special, non-analogical deletion of the hamzah associated with the verb's frequent usage.

f: Why can the exceptional deletion found in رَأَى not simply be applied to يَنْأَى?
b: Because the deletion in رَأَى is an exceptional shortening established by frequent usage, whereas يَنْأَى is not used frequently enough for the same non-analogical deletion to have become established.

f: What broader lesson does the discussion of رَأَى teach about Arabic morphology?
b: A morphological form can have a regular analogical derivation, yet frequent usage may establish an exceptional shortened form. Such lexical exceptions must be distinguished from productive morphological rules.

f: What are the forms of رَأَى when the verb is followed by nūn al-tawkīd al-thaqīlah?
b: The forms given are رَيِنَّ، رَيَانِّ، رَؤُونَّ؛ رَيِنَّ، رَيَانِّ، رَيِنَانِّ according to the respective persons and numbers. The important point is that the deleted final weak radical is restored under nūn al-tawkīd.

f: What happens to the deleted final weak radical of رَأَى when nūn al-tawkīd is attached?
b: The deleted lām of the verb is restored, following the same principle previously discussed for weak verbs such as اغزون.

f: Why is the final weak radical restored in the emphatic forms of رَأَى?
b: The addition of nūn al-tawkīd changes the phonological environment that originally caused the final weak radical to be deleted, so the deleted radical is restored.

f: What are the forms of رَأَى with nūn al-tawkīd al-khafīfah?
b: The passage gives رَيِنْ، رَؤُونْ، رَيِنْ for the applicable forms.

f: What is the active participle of رَأَى?
b: The active participle is رَاءٍ. Its underlying form is رَائِي, which undergoes the same type of weak-letter treatment as رَامٍ.

f: What is the morphological derivation of رَاءٍ as the active participle of رَأَى?
b: The underlying form is رَائِي. The yāʾ is deleted in the masculine singular after the appropriate vowel changes, producing رَاءٍ.

f: What are the dual forms of the active participle رَاءٍ?
b: The dual forms are رَائِيَانِ in the nominative and رَائِيَيْنِ in the accusative/genitive, according to the normal dual inflection.

f: What is the masculine plural active participle of رَأَى?
b: It is رَاؤُونَ in the nominative, with the underlying form رَائِيُونَ undergoing vowel transfer and deletion of the yāʾ.

f: How is رَاؤُونَ derived from رَائِيُونَ?
b: The ḍammah of the yāʾ is transferred to the preceding hamzah, the yāʾ is deleted, and the resulting form is رَاؤُونَ, analyzed on the morphological weight فَاعُونَ.

f: Why does the passage compare رَاءٍ رَائِيَانِ رَاؤُونَ with رَاعٍ رَاعِيَانِ رَاعُونَ?
b: The forms undergo essentially the same weak-letter transformations as the active participle forms of a regular final-weak verb such as رَعَى → رَاعٍ.

f: What is the passive participle of رَأَى?
b: The passive participle is مَرْئِيٌّ.

f: What is the underlying form of مَرْئِيٌّ?
b: Its underlying form is analyzed as مَرْؤُوِيّ. The wāw is changed into yāʾ, the resulting yāʾs are assimilated, and the preceding vowel is changed to kasrah, producing مَرْئِيّ.

f: Why is the passive participle of رَأَى مَرْئِيّ rather than a form retaining the original wāw?
b: The wāw and yāʾ undergo the established weak-letter rules: the wāw changes into yāʾ when followed by a yāʾ in the relevant environment, the yāʾs are assimilated, and the preceding vowel is changed to kasrah.

f: How does the form IV conjugation of رَأَى differ from the corresponding form IV conjugations of other verbs?
b: The form IV derivation of رَأَى is exceptional because it consistently deletes its hamzah, just as the ordinary present يَرَى does. This differs from corresponding forms such as أَنْأَى, which retain their hamzah.

f: What is the form IV past tense derived from رَأَى?
b: It is أَرَى. Its underlying form is أَرْأَى; the hamzah's movement is transferred to the preceding rāʾ and the hamzah is deleted.

f: Why is أَرَى from رَأَى exceptional?
b: Like يَرَى, أَرَى obligatorily deletes the ʿayn hamzah because of the high frequency of the root ر أ ي and the established usage of the shortened forms.

f: What is the form IV present tense derived from رَأَى?
b: It is يُرِي in the relevant conjugation, with the hamzah deleted from the underlying يُرْئِي

f: What is the form IV maṣdar of رَأَى?
b: The standard maṣdar is إِرَاءَة. The passage also permits إِرَاء and mentions إِرَايَة as another attested form.

f: What is the underlying form of إِرَاءَة, the maṣdar of form IV أَرَى?
b: Its underlying form is analyzed as إِرْآء, on the pattern إِفْعَال. The yāʾ is first changed into hamzah because it occurs after an extra alif, after which the hamzah is treated according to the same deletion process found in the verb.

f: Why does إِرْآء become إِرَاءَة?
b: The movement of the hamzah is transferred to the preceding rāʾ, the hamzah is deleted, and a feminine tāʾ is added as compensation for the deleted hamzah, analogous to the compensatory tāʾ in إِقَامَة.

f: Why can the maṣdar of form IV رَأَى be إِرَاء without the compensatory tāʾ?
b: Unlike إِقَامَة, where the corresponding weak letter is not deleted from the verb itself, the hamzah is already deleted in أَرَى. Therefore, the compensatory tāʾ is not obligatory, and إِرَاء is permitted and widely used.

f: Why is إِرَايَة also permitted as a maṣdar of form IV رَأَى?
b: The yāʾ is changed into hamzah only when it occurs in the relevant final position. If the following tāʾ is treated as belonging to a separate word-like element, the yāʾ can remain, producing إِرَايَة.

f: What is the active participle of form IV أَرَى?
b: The passage gives مُرٍ as the shortened active participle, derived from مُرْئِي after deletion of the hamzah and the corresponding weak-letter changes.

f: What are the dual and masculine plural forms of the active participle of أَرَى?
b: They are مُرْيَانِ and مُرُونَ, derived respectively from مُرْئِيَانِ and مُرْئِيُونَ after the hamzah deletion and weak-letter transformations.

f: What is the feminine active participle of form IV أَرَى?
b: It is مُرِيَة. The underlying form is مُرْئِيَة, with the hamzah deleted according to the same exceptional rule.

f: What are the dual feminine forms of the active participle of أَرَى?
b: The dual forms are مُرِيَتَانِ and مُرِيَتَيْنِ.

f: What is the feminine singular past form of form IV أَرَى?
b: It is أَرَتْ, derived from the underlying أَرْأَتْ

f: What is the morphological weight of أَرَتْ in the feminine singular past?
b: It is analyzed on the weight أَفْتْ after the deletion and weak-letter changes described in the passage.

f: What is the feminine active participle of أَرَى?
b: It is مُرِيَة, from the underlying مُرْئِيَة, with the hamzah deleted.

f: What are the dual and plural feminine active participles of أَرَى?
b: They are مُرِيَتَانِ and مُرِيَاتٌ, derived from مُرْئِيَتَانِ and مُرْئِيَاتٌ after deletion of the hamzah.

f: What is the passive participle of form IV أَرَى?
b: The passage gives مُرًى. Its underlying form is مُرْأَي, with the hamzah deleted, the yāʾ changed into alif, and the resulting alif deleted in the singular indefinite form because of the meeting of two sukūns.

f: Why is the final alif of the passive participle مُرًى deleted in the indefinite singular?
b: The yāʾ is first changed into alif, and the resulting alif then meets the sukūn associated with tanwīn. The alif is therefore deleted because of the meeting of two sukūns.

f: How does the active participle of رَأَى behave in the accusative compared with the nominative/genitive?
b: The active participle may retain its yāʾ in the accusative, as in رَأَيْتُ مَرْئِيًا in the relevant paradigm, because the fatḥah is light and permits retention of the weak letter.

f: Why can the active participle of رَأَى retain its yāʾ in the accusative while being shortened in other cases?
b: The fatḥah is light, so it does not create the same phonetic heaviness that causes deletion in the other forms.

f: How does the passive participle of رَأَى differ from its active participle regarding deletion of the final yāʾ?
b: The passive participle مُرًى deletes the final weak letter in all three cases in the singular because the underlying cause for deletion remains present: the weak letter is moving and preceded by a fatḥah.

f: Why does the passive participle مُرًى retain the same shortened form in the nominative, accusative, and genitive?
b: The condition causing deletion—a moving final weak letter preceded by fatḥah—continues to exist in each case. Therefore the weak letter is deleted in all three cases.

f: What is the dual of the passive participle مُرًى?
b: The dual is مُرْيَانِ with fatḥah on the rāʾ, rather than a form with the final yāʾ changed into alif and deleted.

f: Why is the final yāʾ of the dual passive participle مُرْيَانِ not changed into alif?
b: The dual alif requires the preceding letter to have fatḥah. Changing the yāʾ into alif and deleting it would produce a form that could be confused with another construction, especially when the word is annexed.

f: Why would a hypothetical form مُرَانَ create ambiguity?
b: A form such as مُرَانَ could become ambiguous when annexed, because its structure could be confused with a form in which the dual alif itself represents the relevant morphological distinction.

f: What is the masculine plural of the passive participle of form IV أَرَى?
b: The passage gives مُرْؤُونَ

f: What is the feminine passive participle of form IV أَرَى?
b: It is مُرَاة, derived from an underlying form such as مُرْأَيَة, with the final yāʾ changed into alif.

f: What are the dual and plural feminine forms of the passive participle of أَرَى?
b: The forms are مُرَاتَانِ and مُرَيَاتٌ in the relevant paradigm. The passage preserves distinctions in the vowels and weak letters to avoid confusion between the feminine singular, dual, and plural.

f: Why is the final yāʾ retained in the feminine plural passive participle rather than changed into alif?
b: It is retained to prevent confusion with the feminine singular form. Changing and deleting the yāʾ would make the plural too similar to the singular.

f: What is the main reason that the form IV derivations of رَأَى are exceptional?
b: The exceptional behavior is primarily attributed to the frequency of usage of the root ر أ ي, which caused the deletion of its ʿayn hamzah to become established across its form IV derivatives as well.

f: What broader principle connects the exceptional forms يَرَى, أَرَى, and their derivatives?
b: The forms يَرَى and أَرَى, together with their related forms, preserve an established pattern of hamzah deletion rather than following the ordinary forms of comparable hamzated verbs.

f: What is the imperative paradigm of رَأَى according to the original morphological derivation?
b: The imperative is given as ارْأَ، ارْأَيَا، ارْأَوْا؛ ارْأَيْ، ارْأَيَا، ارْأَيْنَ.

f: What is the underlying form of the masculine singular imperative ارْأَ from رَأَى?
b: It is derived from the rejected original form تُؤْرِئُ (as explained in the passage): the present prefix and final weak radical are removed, leaving ارْأَ after the addition of hamzat al-waṣl.

f: What is the underlying form of the masculine dual imperative ارْأَيَا from رَأَى?
b: It is derived from أَرْئِيَا

f: What is the underlying form of the masculine plural imperative ارْأَوْا from رَأَى?
b: The passage analyzes it through an intermediate form أَرْيُوا. The ḍammah of the yāʾ is transferred to the preceding letter and the yāʾ is deleted, producing أَرَوْا and then the corresponding imperative form.

f: Why do the masculine plural and feminine singular imperatives of رَأَى have different underlying structures despite similar surface forms?
b: In the masculine plural, the final wāw is a subject pronoun, whereas in the feminine singular, the yāʾ belongs to the verb. Their surface similarity therefore does not mean that they have the same morphological weight.

f: What is the morphological weight of the feminine singular imperative ارْأَيْ from رَأَى?
b: It is analyzed on the weight اِفْعِي, with the yāʾ functioning as the feminine singular subject pronoun.

f: What are the forms of رَأَى with nūn al-tawkīd al-thaqīlah in the imperative?
b: The passage gives forms such as ارْأَيْنَّ، ارْأَيَانِّ، ارْأَوُنَّ؛ ارْأَيْنَّ، ارْأَيَانِّ، ارْأَيْنَانِّ, applying the previously established rules for restoring the final weak radical and modifying the pronoun markers under emphasis.

f: What happens to the deleted final weak radical of رَأَى when nūn al-tawkīd is attached?
b: The deleted final weak radical is restored, just as in other final-weak verbs such as اغزون.

f: What happens to the wāw of the masculine plural pronoun when nūn al-tawkīd is attached to رَأَى?
b: The wāw is deleted, but its ḍammah is retained as an indication of the deleted wāw, producing the corresponding emphatic form.

f: What happens to the yāʾ of the feminine singular pronoun when nūn al-tawkīd is attached to رَأَى?
b: The yāʾ is deleted, while its kasrah is retained as an indication of the deleted yāʾ.

f: What is the prohibition paradigm of رَأَى with لَا النَّاهِيَة?
b: The passage gives لَا تَرَ، لَا تَرَيَا، لَا تَرَوْا؛ لَا تَرَيْ، لَا تَرَيَا، لَا تَرَيْنَ.

f: What happens to the final weak radical of رَأَى after لَا النَّاهِيَة?
b: It is deleted in the forms where the ordinary jussive rules require its deletion, just as in previously discussed forms such as لَا تَغْزُ and لَا تَرْمِ.

f: What happens when nūn al-tawkīd is added to the prohibited forms of رَأَى?
b: The final weak radical is restored in the singular forms, while the wāw or yāʾ of the relevant pronoun may be deleted with its vowel retained as an indication of it, following the previously established rules.

f: Why does the author provide the full imperative and prohibition paradigms of رَأَى?
b: He provides them to demonstrate that the exceptional hamzah deletion in رَأَى must be combined with the previously established rules governing weak verbs, imperatives, jussives, nūn al-tawkīd, and pronoun suffixes.

f: What is the underlying present-tense form of أَرَى, the form IV verb derived from رَأَى?
b: The underlying form is تُؤَرِئُ

f: How is the present-tense form of form IV أَرَى derived according to the passage?
b: The movement of the ʿayn hamzah is transferred to the preceding rāʾ and the hamzah is deleted, just as in the ordinary present يَرَى.

f: What general rule applies to the unmentioned conjugations and derived forms of hamzated رَأَى?
b: The forms omitted by the author follow the same general rules already established for non-hamzated weak verbs, with the additional exceptional treatment of the hamzah of ر أ ي.

f: What is the general morphological rule for derived forms of رَأَى that the author says should be applied to omitted forms?
b: One should first apply the established weak-verb rules and then apply the special rules governing the hamzah of ر أ ي. The omitted forms are not independent exceptions merely because the author does not list them individually.

f: What is the form VIII (افتعل) derivative of a hamzated-fāʾ verb such as أَلَفَ in the passage's example?
b: The passage gives اِيتَال as an example, analogous to اِخْتَار.

f: What is the form VIII derivative ائْتَلَى and what does it mean?
b: اِيتَلَى means “he fell short, was deficient, or failed to fulfill” in the sense specified by the passage. It is analogous to اِقْتَضَى in its morphological treatment.

f: What are the underlying forms of ايتال and ايتلى?
b: Their underlying forms are ائْتَالَ and ائْتَلَى. The second hamzah is changed into yāʾ because it is sākin and follows a hamzah with kasrah.

f: Why does the author explicitly give the forms ايتال and ايتلى rather than forms with assimilation such as اتّال or اتّلى?
b: He wants to prevent the reader from assuming that the substituted yāʾ behaves like a permanent radical and can therefore undergo the assimilation rules found in forms such as اتَّعَدَ and اتَّسَرَ.

f: Why does the yāʾ in ايتال and ايتلى not become a tāʾ and assimilate into the following tāʾ?
b: Because the yāʾ is only an incidental replacement for hamzah. It is not an original radical and is deleted in many environments, especially when hamzat al-waṣl drops in connected speech.

f: What happens to the yāʾ in ايتال and ايتلى when hamzat al-waṣl drops in connected speech?
b: The yāʾ returns to the original hamzah, because the environment that caused the hamzah-to-yāʾ substitution has disappeared.

f: Why is the form اِتَّزَرَ from اِئْتَزَرَ considered incorrect according to the main analysis in the passage?
b: The yāʾ that would arise from changing the second hamzah is merely incidental and therefore should not be changed into tāʾ and assimilated. The expected form is اِئْتَزَرَ according to the main analogical analysis.

f: Is the form اتَّزَرَ ever found in Arabic despite being rejected by the main analogical analysis?
b: Yes. The cited later authorities report that اتَّزَرَ occurs in transmitted usage, and some grammarians attribute its permissibility to the Kūfans or treat it as restricted to samaʿ rather than productive analogy.

f: Why is اتَّخَذَ not derived from أَخَذَ in the same way as اِئْتَزَرَ would be?
b: اتَّخَذَ is not derived from أَخَذَ. It derives from the separate verb تَخَذَ, meaning “to take,” so the tāʾ can undergo assimilation normally.

f: Why does اتَّخَذَ contain an assimilated tāʾ rather than the form اِيتَخَذَ?
b: Because its underlying root is تَخَذَ, not أَخَذَ. Therefore there is no incidental yāʾ arising from hamzah substitution, and ordinary assimilation applies.

f: What does the chapter on hamzated verbs conclude?
b: The chapter concludes that hamzated verbs generally follow the rules of sound verbs and their corresponding weak categories, but hamzah may undergo special changes such as substitution, easing, or exceptional deletion.

f: What chapter follows the discussion of hamzated verbs?
b: The next chapter is فصل في بناء اسم الزمان والمكان, concerning the formation of nouns of time and place.

f: What is اسم الزمان والمكان?
b: اسم الزمان والمكان is a noun formed to designate the time or place in which an action occurs, without restricting the noun specifically to either time or place.

f: Why is اسم الزمان والمكان described as one of the ألفاظ المشتركة?
b: Because the same form can refer either to a place or to a time, depending on context.

f: What example demonstrates that one noun can denote either a place or a time?
b: مَجْلِس can mean either the place where people sit or the time during which they sit.

f: What pattern is normally used for the active-triliteral verb whose present tense has a kasrah on the ʿayn when forming an ordinary noun of time or place?
b: It is formed on مَفْعِل, with kasrah on the ʿayn, such as مَجْلِس from يَجْلِسُ.

f: Why is مَجْلِس formed on مَفْعِل?
b: Because its present tense يَجْلِسُ has kasrah on the ʿayn, and the noun of place/time follows the same vowel for morphological correspondence (التوافق).

f: What is an example of a non-sound verb whose noun of time or place follows مَفْعِل?
b: مَبِيت is given as an example. It is derived from a final-weak or otherwise non-sound verb, with the appropriate weak-letter transformation.

f: How is مَبِيت derived according to the passage?
b: Its underlying form is مَبْيِت

f: What pattern is normally used for an active-triliteral verb whose present tense has fatḥah on the ʿayn when forming a noun of time or place?
b: It is formed on مَفْعَل, such as مَذْهَب from يَذْهَبُ.

f: What pattern is normally used for an active-triliteral verb whose present tense has ḍammah on the ʿayn when forming a noun of time or place?
b: It is also normally formed on مَفْعَل, such as مَقْتَل from يَقْتُلُ.

f: Why does a present tense with ḍammah on the ʿayn take مَفْعَل rather than مَفْعُل in the noun of time/place?
b: The language does not normally use the pattern مَفْعُل for these nouns. The pattern مَفْعَل is therefore preferred, and its fatḥah is also lighter than kasrah.

f: What example of a noun of time/place from a present tense with ḍammah is given?
b: مَقْتَل from يَقْتُلُ is given as the example.

f: What example of a noun of time/place from a present tense with fatḥah is given?
b: مَشْرَب from يَشْرَبُ is given as an example.

f: What example of a noun of time/place is given from the hollow verb قَامَ يَقُومُ?
b: The noun is مَقَام. Its underlying form is مَقْوَم, which undergoes the same weak-letter treatment as أَقَامَ.

f: How is مَقَام derived from قَامَ يَقُومُ?
b: Its underlying form is مَقْوَم. The middle weak wāw undergoes the appropriate hollow-verb transformation, producing مَقَام.

f: Why does مَقَام not follow the ordinary surface pattern مَفْعَل directly?
b: Because قَامَ is a hollow verb, so its underlying middle weak radical undergoes iʿlāl. The resulting form is مَقَام rather than a form preserving the original wāw.

f: What is the expected pattern for the noun of time/place when the triliteral verb is sound in both its first and last radicals?
b: For a sound verb, the noun of time/place generally follows مَفْعِل when the present has kasrah on the ʿayn, and مَفْعَل when the present has fatḥah or ḍammah on the ʿayn.

f: Which nouns of time/place are exceptions because they have kasrah on the ʿayn despite coming from verbs whose present has fatḥah or ḍammah?
b: The passage lists المَسْجِد، المَشْرِق، المَغْرِب، المَطْلِع، المَجْزِر، المَرْفِق، المَفْرِق، المَسْكِن، المَنْسِك، المَنْبِت، المَسْقِط.

f: Why is the kasrah in words such as المَسْجِد and المَغْرِب considered irregular?
b: Their verbs have a present ʿayn with fatḥah or ḍammah, so according to the regular rule their noun of time/place should have fatḥah on the ʿayn, i.e. the pattern مَفْعَل, rather than مَفْعِل.

f: What is the regular expected form of المَجْزِر according to its verb?
b: Since it comes from يَجْزَرُ with fatḥah on the ʿayn, the regular analogy would give مَجْزَر with fatḥah. The commonly transmitted مَجْزِر is therefore anomalous.

f: What are the meanings of some of the exceptional nouns of time/place listed in the passage?
b: المَجْزِر = place where camels are slaughtered; المَرْفِق = place associated with comfort/ease; المَفْرِق = place of separation, especially the parting of the hair; المَسْكِن = place of dwelling; المَنْسِك = place of worship/ritual; المَنْبِت = place where plants grow; المَسْقِط = place of falling, as in مَسْقِط الرَّأْس.

f: Is the fatḥah pronunciation found for any of these exceptional nouns?
b: Yes. The passage says that fatḥah is transmitted for some of them, specifically المَسْجِد، المَسْكِن، المَطْلِع, in accordance with the regular analogy.

f: Is fatḥah permissible for all the exceptional nouns of time/place?
b: Yes. The passage cites Ibn al-Sikkīt as saying that fatḥah is permissible in all of them according to analogy, even though the author did not hear the fatḥah transmitted for every individual word.

f: What is the rule for the noun of time/place when the verb is weak in its first radical?
b: When the verb has a weak fāʾ, the noun of time/place is formed with kasrah on the ʿayn: مَفْعِل.

f: What examples illustrate the rule for verbs weak in the first radical?
b: المَوْضِع from وَضَعَ, and المَوْعِد from وَعَدَ.

f: Why does the noun of time/place from a fāʾ-weak verb have kasrah on the ʿayn?
b: The passage attributes it to ease of pronunciation. The kasrah is considered easier in this environment, as supported by linguistic usage.

f: Are there dialectal exceptions to the rule that a fāʾ-weak noun of time/place has kasrah?
b: Yes. The passage reports that مُؤَجَّل/مُؤْجَل-type forms with fatḥah have been heard, including reports attributed to al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ. Such forms are treated as exceptional to the general rule.

f: What poetic evidence is cited for a fatḥah in a noun of time/place from a fāʾ-weak verb?
b: A verse transmitted by al-Kisāʾī contains المُؤْجَل with the exceptional vowel. The passage uses it as evidence that fatḥah has been transmitted despite the general kasrah rule.

f: What is the rule for the noun of time/place when the verb is weak in its final radical?
b: When the verb is weak in its lām, the noun of time/place has fatḥah on the ʿayn, regardless of whether the verb's present ʿayn has fatḥah, ḍammah, or kasrah, and regardless of whether the final weak radical is wāwī or yāʾī.

f: Why does a lām-weak noun of time/place always have fatḥah on the ʿayn?
b: The final weak radical undergoes transformation into alif, and this produces the fixed pattern with fatḥah before the final alif.

f: What examples illustrate the rule for lām-weak nouns of time/place?
b: المَأْوَى and المَرْمَى are given as examples.

f: Why does the author give both المَأْوَى and المَرْمَى as examples?
b: To show that the rule applies whether the verb's final weak radical is wāw or yāʾ, and whether the ʿayn itself is weak or sound.

f: Are there transmitted forms with kasrah instead of fatḥah for some lām-weak nouns of time/place?
b: Yes. مَأْوِي الإبل and مَأْقِي العين are reported with kasrah. These are treated as transmitted variants against the general rule of fatḥah.

f: What question arises when a verb is weak in both its first and final radicals?
b: Since a fāʾ-weak verb takes kasrah in its noun of time/place and a lām-weak verb takes fatḥah, one may ask what happens when the verb is weak in both positions: should its noun of time/place have kasrah or fatḥah?

f: What conclusion does the passage reach about a verb weak in both its first and final radicals?
b: The passage reports that some later authorities treat it as having fatḥah, following the rule of the lām-weak verb. Thus it is treated like the nāqiṣ in this respect.

f: What example is given for the noun of time/place of a verb weak in both its first and final radicals?
b: مَأْقَى with fatḥah on the qāf is cited as the reported rule.

f: Which later authorities are mentioned as indicating that a fāʾ-and-lām-weak noun of time/place takes fatḥah?
b: The passage mentions al-Sakkākī in the Miftāḥ al-ʿUlūm as indicating this rule.

f: What is the general distinction between the rules for fāʾ-weak and lām-weak nouns of time/place?
b: Fāʾ-weak → kasrah on the ʿayn; lām-weak → fatḥah on the ʿayn. When both are weak, the passage reports the lām-weak rule, namely fatḥah.

f: Can اسم الزمان والمكان take feminine tāʾ?
b: Yes. Some nouns of time/place can take tāʾ al-taʾnīth, either for intensification or to designate a particular place/boundary (buqʿah).

f: Is the use of feminine tāʾ in nouns of time/place governed by productive analogy?
b: The passage says that such forms are restricted to transmitted usage (samāʿ) rather than being freely generated by analogy.

f: What examples of nouns of time/place with feminine tāʾ are given?
b: المَظِنَّة = the place in which something is thought or suspected; المَقْبَرَة = a place where people are buried; المَشْرِقَة = a place where the sun rises/shines.

f: What is the regular pattern of المَقْبَرَة and المَشْرِقَة?
b: According to the verb-based analogy, their ʿayn should have fatḥah, because their underlying verbs belong to the category with a ḍammah on the present ʿayn.

f: What irregular forms of المَقْبَرَة and المَشْرِقَة are mentioned?
b: المُقْبُرَة / المَقْبُرَة-type and المُشْرُقَة

f: Why might a form such as المَقْبُرَة with ḍammah not really be considered an irregular derivative from the verb?
b: Ibn al-Ḥājib explains that forms on مَفْعُلَة with ḍammah can be nouns that are not actually derived according to the verb's pattern. They can instead function like independently established nouns such as قَارُورَة.

f: How does the meaning differ between a verb-derived place noun and an independently designated place noun on مَفْعُلَة?
b: The verb-derived form denotes the place where the action actually occurs. The independently designated form can denote a place specifically prepared, designated, or characterized for that action.

f: How does this distinction apply to المَقْبَرَة?
b: With مَقْبَرَة on the regular pattern, it denotes the place where burial occurs. With the anomalous مَقْبُرَة interpretation, it can refer to a specific area designated or established as a burial place.

f: How does this distinction apply to المَشْرِقَة?
b: The verb-derived meaning concerns the place where the sun actually rises or shines, whereas the independently designated interpretation can refer to a place specifically prepared or designated for exposure to the sun.

f: Why does the author say that المَظِنَّة itself should technically be considered anomalous?
b: المَظِنَّة has kasrah on the ʿayn, while it comes from يَظُنُّ with ḍammah. According to the ordinary rule, its noun of time/place should have fatḥah, so its kasrah is also technically a deviation from analogy.

f: What is the overall principle governing irregular nouns of time/place in this passage?
b: The regular patterns are based on the present-tense vowel and the presence of weak radicals, but actual Arabic usage includes many lexicalized exceptions. Some variants are transmitted by hearing, while others may represent nouns that have become independent from the productive verbal pattern.

f: How are nouns of time and place formed from verbs having more than three original or total radicals?
b: They are formed on the same pattern as the passive participle of the verb. This applies whether the verb is a derived triliteral, a basic quadriliteral, or a derived quadriliteral.

f: Why does اسم الزمان والمكان from a verb with more than three letters follow the passive participle?
b: The passive participle is lighter in pronunciation and semantically appropriate because the noun of time/place designates where or when an action is performed, making its meaning similar to something upon which an action occurs.

f: What examples illustrate nouns of time/place formed like passive participles from verbs with more than three letters?
b: Examples include المُدْخَل، المُقَام، المُدَحْرَج، المُنْطَلَق، المُسْتَخْرَج، and المُحْرَنْجَم.

f: What does المُحْرَنْجَم mean in the cited example?
b: It refers to a place where camels have gathered together.

f: What is the pattern used when something is abundant in a particular place?
b: From a basic triliteral verb, the pattern مَفْعَلَة is used, with fatḥah on the mīm, ʿayn, and tāʾ, and sukūn on the fāʾ.

f: What does the pattern مَفْعَلَة indicate when applied to a place?
b: It indicates a place in which something is abundant or plentiful.

f: Is the pattern مَفْعَلَة for a place of abundance built directly from a derived verb?
b: No. If the relevant word is derived from a verb with additional letters, it is first reduced to its basic triliteral form, and the pattern مَفْعَلَة is then constructed from that basic form.

f: What are examples of مَفْعَلَة indicating a place abundant in something?
b: أَرْضٌ مَسْبَعَة = land with many wild beasts; مَأْسَدَة = a place with many lions; مَذْأَبَة = a place with many wolves; مَبْطَخَة = a place with many watermelons; مَقْثَاة = a place with many cucumbers.

f: How is مَسْبَعَة derived?
b: It is derived from the basic verb/noun سَبُع in the sense relevant to the passage, producing مَسْبَعَة, meaning a place abundant in wild beasts.

f: How is مَأْسَدَة derived?
b: It is derived from أَسَد, producing مَأْسَدَة, meaning a place abundant in lions.

f: How is مَذْأَبَة derived?
b: It is derived from ذِئْب, producing مَذْأَبَة, meaning a place abundant in wolves.

f: How is مَبْطَخَة derived from بَطِّيخ?
b: Because بَطِّيخ is not itself a basic triliteral form for this derivational purpose, the relevant basic form is used and the extra letters are removed, yielding مَبْطَخَة, meaning a place abundant in watermelons.

f: How is مَقْثَاة derived from قِثَّاء?
b: The derived noun is reduced to the appropriate basic form, with one of the doubled/thickened consonants and the extra alif removed, producing مَقْثَاة, meaning a place abundant in cucumbers.

f: Is the reading مَطْبَخَة mentioned in the passage reliable?
b: The passage says that a manuscript contains مَطْبَخَة, but considers this an error. It can only be interpreted by taking الطَّبِيخ as a dialectal form of البَطِّيخ.

f: What dialectal word does the passage mention as a synonym for بَطِّيخ?
b: طَبِيخ is reported as a dialectal form of بَطِّيخ, particularly associated with the people of the Ḥijāz.

f: What hadith is cited for the word الطبيخ?
b: A report from ʿĀʾishah says that the Prophet ﷺ used to eat الطَّبِيخ with fresh dates.

f: Can the مَفْعَلَة pattern of place abundance be formed from a quadriliteral verb or noun?
b: No. If the relevant noun is quadriliteral, whether basic or derived, this pattern is not constructed from it because doing so would result in excessive morphological heaviness.

f: What examples are given of quadriliteral words from which مَفْعَلَة is not constructed?
b: ثَعْلَب and عُصْفُور are given as examples of words with more than three letters. Instead of constructing a special form, one simply says كَثِيرَةُ الثَّعَالِب or كَثِيرَةُ العَصَافِير, according to the intended meaning.

f: Can مَفْعَلَة be constructed from a five-letter noun?
b: No. Five-letter nouns such as جَخْمَرِش and عُضْرَفُوط are too heavy for this derivational pattern, so abundance is expressed descriptively instead.

f: What is اسم الآلة?
b: اسم الآلة is the noun designating something by which an agent acts upon an object so that the effect of the action reaches that object.

f: What is meant by “the effect of the action reaches the object” in the definition of اسم الآلة?
b: The instrument must be used in a transitive, manipulable action in which something is acted upon. For example, a carpenter uses a tool on wood, causing the action's effect to reach the wood.

f: What example does the passage give to illustrate اسم الآلة?
b: المِنْحَت is given as an example: it is the tool with which a carpenter works upon wood.

f: Why is the definition of الآلة phrased using the masculine pronoun هو even though الآلة is feminine?
b: The pronoun refers to the explanatory phrase ما يُعالج به الفاعل المفعول, which is grammatically masculine. It therefore permits either الآلة هي ما... or الآلة هو ما... according to what the pronoun is taken to refer to.

f: Why can the definition of الآلة not simply be understood as defining اسم الآلة itself?
b: The definition properly describes the instrument itself, not the grammatical noun that names it. Treating it as a definition of the name would require an omitted word such as “اسم الآلة اسم ما يُعالج به,” which is problematic.

f: Why would defining اسم الآلة as “the name of what the agent uses on the object” be problematic?
b: Such a definition would potentially include ordinary tools such as القَدُوم, even though the technical category of اسم الآلة is concerned with specific morphological noun patterns rather than every possible tool name.

f: What kind of actions can technically have an اسم آلة?
b: اسم الآلة is associated with transitive, manipulable actions, because the definition requires an object upon which the action's effect is produced. Purely intransitive actions do not normally have an instrument in this technical sense.

f: What patterns of اسم الآلة does the passage mention?
b: The passage mentions مِفْعَل, مِفْعَلَة, and مِفْعَال. Examples include مِخْلَب, مِكْسَحَة, and مِفْتَاح.

f: What is an example of اسم الآلة on the pattern مِفْعَل?
b: مِخْلَب is given as an example.

f: What is an example of اسم الآلة on the pattern مِفْعَلَة?
b: مِكْسَحَة is given as an example. The passage says that this pattern, with the added tāʾ, is restricted to transmitted usage (samāʿ).

f: What is an example of اسم الآلة on the pattern مِفْعَال?
b: مِفْتَاح is given as an example.

f: Why does the author mention مِصْفَاة as an example of اسم الآلة?
b: Although its surface form does not immediately look identical to مِكْسَحَة, it belongs to the same مِفْعَلَة pattern historically. Its underlying form is مِصْفَوَة, from which the wāw changes into alif, producing مِصْفَاة.

f: What is مِصْفَاة used for?
b: It is an instrument for filtering or straining, hence its classification as اسم الآلة.

f: What are the two possible forms of مَرْقَاة mentioned in the passage?
b: مِرْقَاة with kasrah on the mīm is treated as an instrument, while مَرْقَاة with fatḥah on the mīm is treated as a place.

f: Why can مِرْقَاة with kasrah on the mīm be اسم آلة?
b: It denotes something by which one ascends, such as a ladder or means of climbing. It therefore functions as an instrument of the action.

f: Why can مَرْقَاة with fatḥah on the mīm denote a place instead?
b: With fatḥah on the mīm, it is interpreted as the place where climbing occurs, rather than the instrument used for climbing.

f: What other words exhibit the same distinction between an instrument and a place?
b: The passage mentions مَطْهَرَة/مِطْهَرَة, مَرْقَاة/مِرْقَاة, and مَسْقَاة/مِسْقَاة, where the vowel of the mīm can indicate whether the word is understood as a place or as an instrument.

f: What does Ibn al-Sikkīt say about the forms مَطْهَرَة/مِطْهَرَة, مَرْقَاة/مِرْقَاة, and مَسْقَاة/مِسْقَاة?
b: He explains that the kasrah is used when the word is understood as an instrument, analogous to other instrument nouns, while the fatḥah is used when it is understood as a place in which the action occurs.

f: What are the two semantic perspectives that explain the forms مِرْقَاة and مَرْقَاة?
b: A ladder can be viewed as a place of climbing, because climbing occurs upon it, or as an instrument of climbing, because it enables the act of climbing.

f: Do مِرْقَاة and مَرْقَاة necessarily refer to two different physical objects?
b: No. The passage explains that both forms can refer to the same thing, such as a ladder. The difference lies in the speaker's perspective and intended semantic classification: place versus instrument.

f: What is the key distinction between the kasrah and fatḥah in forms such as مِرْقَاة and مَرْقَاة?
b: Kasrah on the mīm indicates that the object is being considered as an instrument (اسم آلة), while fatḥah on the mīm indicates that it is being considered as a place (اسم مكان).

f: Which nouns are anomalous as instrument nouns because they have ḍammah on both the mīm and ʿayn?
b: The passage lists مُدْهُن، مُسْعُط، مُدُقّ، مُنْخُل، مُكْحُلَة، مُخْرُضَة with ḍammah on the mīm and ʿayn, contrary to the expected instrument-noun patterns.

f: What does مُدْهُن mean?
b: مُدْهُن is the container in which oil (الدهن) is kept.

f: What does مُسْعُط mean?
b: مُسْعُط is the container in which snuff (السعوط) is kept.

f: What does مُدُقّ mean?
b: مُدُقّ is an instrument with which something is pounded.

f: What does مُنْخُل mean?
b: مُنْخُل is an instrument with which something is sifted.

f: What does مُكْحُلَة mean?
b: مُكْحُلَة is the container in which kohl (الكحل) is kept.

f: What does مُخْرُضَة mean?
b: مُخْرُضَة is the container in which الأشنان is kept.

f: What is the expected vowel pattern for an ordinary instrument noun, compared with forms such as مُدْهُن and مُنْخُل?
b: The regular pattern has kasrah on the mīm and fatḥah on the ʿayn, such as مِفْعَل and مِفْعَلَة. Thus the listed forms with ḍammah on the mīm and ʿayn are outwardly contrary to the productive pattern.

f: Are all of the nouns مُدْهُن، مُسْعُط، مُدُقّ، مُنْخُل، مُكْحُلَة، مُخْرُضَة genuinely anomalous instrument nouns?
